s: Zichan of Zheng, in the Zuozhuan (Duke Zhao 7, 535 BCE), says a person's first transformation at birth is called po 魄 and, once po is born, its yang is called hun 魂; by using many refined things the hun and po grow strong until they reach shen ming 神明, spirit-brightness.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1901, The Religious System of China, Vol. 4: The Soul in Philosophy and Folk-Conception
src.q: 子產曰、能、人生始化曰魄、既生魄陽曰魂、用物精多則魂魄強、是以有精爽至於神明

src.l: James Legge (trans.), Zuo Qiuming (attrib.), 1872, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5, Part 2: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen (Dukes Seang–Gae)
src.loc: Zuozhuan Zhao 7, Legge's English, p. 618; scan 218
src.q: When a man is born, [we see] in his first movements what is called the animal soul. After this has been produced, it is developed into what is called the spirit.

s: Zichan (Zuozhuan, Zhao 7, 535 BCE) explains the ghost of Boyou: when an ordinary man or woman dies a violent death (強死), their hun and po can still cling to people and act as a malignant spirit (厲), and a ghost with a place to go to does not become one, so Zichan gave Boyou's line an heir to sacrifice.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1901, The Religious System of China, Vol. 4: The Soul in Philosophy and Folk-Conception
src.q: 匹夫匹婦强死、其魂魄猶能馮依於人、以為淫厲

src.l: James Legge (trans.), Zuo Qiuming (attrib.), 1872, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5, Part 2: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen (Dukes Seang–Gae)
src.q: When a ghost has a place to go to, it does not become an evil spirit. I have made such a place for the ghost.

src.l: James Legge (trans.), Zuo Qiuming (attrib.), 1872, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5, Part 2: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen (Dukes Seang–Gae)
src.q: When an ordinary man or woman dies a violent death, the soul and spirit are still able to keep hanging about men in the shape of an evil apparition

s: Legge's English of the Zuozhuan (1872) renders 魄 po 'the animal soul', 魂 hun 'the spirit', and the pair 魂魄 'the soul and spirit', so that 'soul' moves from po to the compound within one speech, and 'spirit' takes the hun although the text keeps 神 shen for a further stage (至於神明).

src.l: James Legge (trans.), Zuo Qiuming (attrib.), 1872, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5, Part 2: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen (Dukes Seang–Gae)
src.q: what is called the animal soul. After this has been produced, it is developed into what is called the spirit. By the use of things the subtle elements are multiplied, and the soul and spirit become strong.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1901, The Religious System of China, Vol. 4: The Soul in Philosophy and Folk-Conception
src.q: 人生始化曰魄、既生魄陽曰魂、用物精多則魂魄強

s: De Groot (The Religious System of China IV, 1901) treats hun and po as one soul in two parts: the compounds kwei-shen 鬼神 and hwun-p'oh 魂魄 add no new idea and 'simply denote the soul in its two component parts'; he speaks of 'the dual soul'.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1901, The Religious System of China, Vol. 4: The Soul in Philosophy and Folk-Conception
src.q: Thus we have kwei-shen and hwun-p'oh, which are combinations of nouns, simply denoting the soul in its two component parts.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1901, The Religious System of China, Vol. 4: The Soul in Philosophy and Folk-Conception
src.q: the part the dual soul plays while still residing in the living human body

s: The Liji (Jiaotesheng; Warring States–Han), as cited by Ye Mengde (1077–1148) in the Qianlong Liji yishu, says the hun-qi returns to heaven and the form-po returns to earth: what returns to heaven is the knowing qi rising, what returns to earth is the body-po descending.

src.l: 高宗弘曆 Qianlong emperor (commissioned), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 欽定禮記義疏·卷六十一 (vol 77)
src.loc: juan 61, Jiyi commentary, 葉氏夢得; scan 8
src.q: 郊特牲 謂魂氣歸於天形魄歸於地歸於天者知氣升自上 也歸於地者體魄降自下也

src.l: 衞湜 Wei Shi, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 禮記集說·卷一百十二 (vol 138)
src.loc: Wei Shi, Liji jishuo juan 112; scan 16
src.q: 氣歸于天形魄歸于地以是而巳魂亦神也

s: The Liji's Jiyi chapter, with Zheng Xuan's (127–200) note as cited in the Liji yishu (1748), says qi is the fullness of shen and po the fullness of gui; Zheng glosses breathing in and out as qi and the acuity of ear and eye as po.

src.l: 高宗弘曆 Qianlong emperor (commissioned), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 欽定禮記義疏·卷六十一 (vol 77)
src.q: 魄也者鬼之盛也鄭氏注曰嘘吸出入者氣也 耳目之聰明為魄氣則魂之謂也

s: The Huainanzi (139 BCE), quoted in the Liji yishu with Gao You's (fl. 205–212) note, says the qi of heaven is hun and the qi of earth is po; Gao glosses hun as a person's yang shen and po as a person's yin shen.

src.l: 高宗弘曆 Qianlong emperor (commissioned), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 欽定禮記義疏·卷六十一 (vol 77)
src.q: 淮南子曰天氣為 魂地氣為魄髙誘注曰魂人陽神也魄人隂神也

s: The Huangdi neijing Lingshu, ch. 8 'Benshen' (Han), as printed in Ma Shi's Ming commentary (1586): when two essences clash it is called shen; what comes and goes with the shen is called hun; what goes in and out with the essence (jing) is called po; what takes charge of things is called the heart-mind (xin).

src.l: attributed to Huangdi, 1587, Commentary on the Yellow Emperor's Classic: Spiritual Pivot (Huangdi Neijing Lingshu), Vol 1
src.q: 兩精相搏謂之神隨神徃來者謂之魂並

src.l: attributed to Huangdi, 1587, Commentary on the Yellow Emperor's Classic: Spiritual Pivot (Huangdi Neijing Lingshu), Vol 1
src.q: 精而出入者謂之魄所以任物者謂之心

src.l: attributed to Huangdi, 1587, Commentary on the Yellow Emperor's Classic: Spiritual Pivot (Huangdi Neijing Lingshu), Vol 1
src.q: That which is called the ethereal soul hún (魂) belongs to Yang; yet the ethereal soul goes and comes following Spirit.

s: The medical scheme of the five viscera, as excerpted in Zeng Zao's Leishuo (1136), lodges shen in the heart, po in the lungs, hun in the liver, yi (intent) in the spleen and zhi (will) in the kidneys; De Groot (1901) calls the liver 'the chief store of the hwun'.

src.l: 曾慥 Zeng Zao, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 類說·卷三十七~卷三十八 (vol 18)
src.q: 心藏神肺藏魄肝藏魂脾藏意腎藏志是為五臟所 藏

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1901, The Religious System of China, Vol. 4: The Soul in Philosophy and Folk-Conception
src.q: the shape of the liver is that of a “dragon, and it is the chief store of the h w u n”

s: The Xingli daquan (1415), juan 28 'Guishen', glosses shen 神 as 'extending' (伸), qi on its way out and growing, and gui 鬼 as 'returning' (歸), qi already receding; heaven, spring-summer, day, the rising tide are shen, and earth, autumn-winter, night, the ebb are gui.

src.l: 胡廣 Hu Guang (ed.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 性理大全書·卷二十八 (vol 18)
src.q: 大抵神之為言伸也伸是氣之方長者也 鬼之為言歸也歸是氣之巳退者也

src.l: 胡廣 Hu Guang (ed.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 性理大全書·卷二十八 (vol 18)
src.q: 凡氣之伸者皆為陽屬 神凡氣之屈者皆為隂屬鬼

s: Zhu Xi (1130–1200), in the imperial Zhuzi quanshu (1713), says gui and shen are only qi, what bends and stretches, goes and comes; a person's qi is continuous with the qi of heaven and earth, so the stirring of the heart reaches it; day is shen and night gui, life is shen and death gui.

src.l: 朱熹 Zhu Xi, 李光地 Li Guangdi (ed.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 御纂朱子全書·卷五十~卷五十一 (vol 88)
src.q: 鬼神只是氣屈伸往来者氣也天地間無非氣人之氣 與天地之氣常相接無間斷

src.l: 朱熹 Zhu Xi, 李光地 Li Guangdi (ed.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 御纂朱子全書·卷五十~卷五十一 (vol 88)
src.q: 如日為神夜為鬼生 為神死為鬼

s: Asked how the dead ancestors can be reached in sacrifice, Zhu Xi (Zhuzi quanshu, 1713) answers that the ancestors' qi is continuous with one's own; their qi is still there, and when the descendant brings his own qi and spirit to bear with sincerity, it gathers and comes.

src.l: 朱熹 Zhu Xi, 李光地 Li Guangdi (ed.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 御纂朱子全書·卷五十~卷五十一 (vol 88)
src.q: 蓋祖考之氣與己連續

src.l: 朱熹 Zhu Xi, 李光地 Li Guangdi (ed.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 御纂朱子全書·卷五十~卷五十一 (vol 88)
src.q: 祖先巳死以何而求曰其氣亦自在只是以我之 氣承接其氣才致精神以求之便来格

s: Zhu Xi (Zhuzi quanshu, 1713) says all that can remember is what po stores and receives, and what issues out into use is hun; what can perceive is po, and perception issuing out is hun; broadly po belongs to the body and hun to the spirit (精神), so jing is po and shen is hun.

src.l: 朱熹 Zhu Xi, 李光地 Li Guangdi (ed.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 御纂朱子全書·卷三十六~卷三十七 (vol 81)
src.q: 凡能記憶皆魄之所藏受也至於 運用發出來是魂

src.l: 朱熹 Zhu Xi, 李光地 Li Guangdi (ed.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 御纂朱子全書·卷三十六~卷三十七 (vol 81)
src.q: 或曰大率魄屬形體魂屬精神曰精又 是魄神又是魂

s: A gloss on Zichan in the Xingli daquan (1415), juan 28, says po forms as the embryo first takes shape and hun is its first stirring; a person's knowing and perceiving belong to hun and the bodily frame to po; hun is the numen of yang and flower of qi, po the numen of yin and essence of the body.

src.l: 胡廣 Hu Guang (ed.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 性理大全書·卷二十八 (vol 18)
src.q: 故人之知覺屬魂形體屬魄陽為魂隂 為魄魂者陽之靈而氣之英魄者隂之靈而體之精

s: Zhang Zai (1020–1077), quoted in Wei Shi's Liji jishuo (1226), says gui and shen are the innate capacity (良能) of the two qi; Gu Yanwu's Rizhilu (1670) quotes his Zhengmeng that the Great Void cannot but have qi, qi cannot but gather into the myriad things, and things cannot but disperse back into the Great Void.

src.l: 衞湜 Wei Shi, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 禮記集說·卷一百十二~卷一百十三 (vol 56)
src.q: 鬼神天地之功用張橫渠曰鬼神二氣之良能

src.l: 顧炎武 Gu Yanwu, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 日知錄·卷一 (vol 1)
src.loc: Rizhilu juan 1, 游魂為變; scan 195
src.q: 張 子正蒙有云太虛不能無氣氣不能不聚而為萬物萬 物不能不散而為太虛

s: Gu Yanwu (Rizhilu, 1670) reads the Yijing's 'essence-qi makes things, the wandering hun makes change' as going from nothing to something and from something to nothing; he quotes Zhang Zai that gui means return, qi dispersing into the formless, and records that Lü Nan refuted Chen Shidao's reading of 'wandering hun' as transmigration.

src.l: 顧炎武 Gu Yanwu, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 日知錄·卷一 (vol 1)
src.q: 精氣為物自無而之有也游魂為變自有而之無也

src.l: 顧炎武 Gu Yanwu, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 日知錄·卷一 (vol 1)
src.q: 鬼者歸也張子曰氣之為物散入無形適得吾體此之 謂歸 陳無已 師 道 以游魂為變為輪廻之說 理 究 呂仲木 柟辨之

s: Fan Zhen (c. 450–515), in the Shenmie lun 'The Spirit Perishes' (preserved in Sengyou's Hongmingji, c. 515), says spirit and body are different names for one thing: spirit is to the body's substance as sharpness to a blade; without sharpness there is no blade, and no one has heard of the blade gone and the sharpness remaining, so how could the body perish and the spirit remain.

src.l: 僧祐 Sengyou (comp.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 弘明集·卷八~卷九: Hong Ming Ji (vol 4)
src.loc: juan 9, Xiao Chen, 難范縝神滅論 (Fan Zhen's text quoted); scan 67
src.q: 問曰名既已殊體何得一荅曰神之於質猶利之於刃 形之於用猶刃之於利利之名非刃也刃之名非利也 然而捨利無刃捨刃無利未聞刃没而利存豈容形亡 而神在

src.l: 僧祐 Sengyou (comp.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 弘明集·卷八~卷九: Hong Ming Ji (vol 4)
src.q: 思文啓竊見范縝神滅論自為賔主遂有三十餘條

s: A text in the Hongmingji (c. 515, juan 5), attributed to Huiyuan (334–416) as 'The Body Ends, the Spirit Does Not Perish' (形盡神不滅; the attribution is not on the scanned span): the passing of fire to firewood is like the passing of spirit to body; fire passes to other wood as spirit to other bodies; the deluded, seeing the body rot in one life, think spirit and feeling perish together, like seeing a fire end in one log.

src.l: 僧祐 Sengyou (comp.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 弘明集·卷三~卷五: Hong Ming Ji (vol 2)
src.q: 火之傳於 薪猶神之傳於形火之傳異薪猶神之傳異形

src.l: 僧祐 Sengyou (comp.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 弘明集·卷三~卷五: Hong Ming Ji (vol 2)
src.q: 惑者見形朽於一生便以謂神情俱喪猶覩火窮於一 木謂終期都盡耳

s: Another defender of the spirit's survival in the Hongmingji (juan 5, c. 515) answers the objection that without the body the spirit has nowhere to lodge: fire exists with firewood and not without, but firewood is not the root of fire; fire is fire's own root and only uses the wood, as spirit and body depend on each other in life.

src.l: 僧祐 Sengyou (comp.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 弘明集·卷三~卷五: Hong Ming Ji (vol 2)
src.q: 夫火因薪則有火無薪則無火薪雖所以生火而非火 之本火本自在因薪為用耳

s: Answering Emperor Wu of Liang's rescript against the Shenmie lun (c. 507), Shen Yue (441–513) writes in the Hongmingji that 'the spirit is originally imperishable' is what he has long held, and that talk of the spirit perishing truly alarms him; Fan Xiu likewise thanks the emperor for answering the court on the Shenmie lun.

src.l: 僧祐 Sengyou (comp.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 弘明集·卷十~卷十一: Hong Ming Ji (vol 5)
src.q: 神本不滅乆所伏膺神滅之談良用駭惕

src.l: 僧祐 Sengyou (comp.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 弘明集·卷十~卷十一: Hong Ming Ji (vol 5)
src.q: 伏見詔㫖所答臣下審神滅論

s: The Tianzhong ji (Chen Yaowen, 1569) explains the Chuci 'Zhaohun' (Summoning the Soul, 3rd c. BCE) after Wang Yi: Song Yu wrote it pitying Qu Yuan, whose life was about to fall, to bring back his essence-spirit (精神) and lengthen his years; it glosses hun as 'the essence of the body' (身之精).

src.l: 陳耀文 Chen Yaowen, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 天中記·卷二十三 (vol 23)
src.q: 招魂招魂者宋玉之所作也魂者身之精也宋玉憐哀 屈原厥命將落作招魂欲以復其精神延其年壽也

s: The Tianzhong ji (1569) records from the Jin zhongxing shu that when Princess Pei called back the soul of Sima Yue, whose coffin had burned, and buried it, Emperor Yuan of Jin banned summoned-soul burials: 'the tomb stores the form, the temple settles the spirit'; to bury a summoned soul is to bury the spirit.

src.l: 陳耀文 Chen Yaowen, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 天中記·卷二十三 (vol 23)
src.q: 夫冢以藏形廟以安神令 世招魂葬者是埋神也其禁之

s: Daoshi's Fayuan zhulin (668) explains the rite of calling the dead with their garment: the hun has gone out, so the clothes call the hun, which knows its own garment and follows it back to the po of the corpse; if the floss at the mouth stirs, the hun has returned; hence one says 'summon the hun', never 'call the po'.

src.l: 道世 Daoshi, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 法苑珠林·卷一百十四~卷一百十六: Fayuan Zhulin (vol 42)
src.q: 以魂外出故將衣喚魂魂識巳衣 尋衣歸魄若魂歸於魄則屍口纊動

src.l: 道世 Daoshi, n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 法苑珠林·卷一百十四~卷一百十六: Fayuan Zhulin (vol 42)
src.q: 故云招魂不言喚魄

s: De Groot (Religious System of China I, 1892) describes a Buddhist priest at Amoy summoning the dead person's soul into the ancestral tablet with a hand-bell and a quatrain: 'Doubt not, soul of the deceased, but hearken from afar'.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1892, The Religious System of China, Vol. 1
src.loc: ch. Summoning the Soul into the Tablet, p. 73; scan 115
src.q: Doubt not, soul of the deceased, but hearken from afar and > understand the meaning thereof

s: A Daoist commentary in the Daozong liushu (1576) says the three hun are the true Original Spirit (元神) and the seven po are the seven emotions, joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate and desire; a whole hun makes an immortal, a whole po makes a ghost, and hun and po standing together make a human.

src.l: various (Daoist); incl. 譚峭 Tan Qiao, 1576, 道宗六書 :6種, 36卷. [China] : 黄世厚, 明萬曆丙子 [4年, 1576].
src.loc: 先天道德經 juan 2, marginal commentary; scan 100
src.q: 所謂三 魂者即此元神真而七魄者喜怒哀懼愛惡欲也 全魂即為仙全魄即為鬼魂與魄兩立則為人

src.l: various (Daoist); incl. 譚峭 Tan Qiao, 1576, 道宗六書 :6種, 36卷. [China] : 黄世厚, 明萬曆丙子 [4年, 1576].
src.q: The seven physical souls are the emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hatred, and desire. A complete spiritual soul makes one an immortal. A complete physical soul makes one a ghost.

s: The Guan Yinzi (attrib. Zhou, compiled Tang–Song), quoted in the Daozong liushu (1576), says ordinary people use po to hold hun and the sage uses hun to move po; by day the hun lodges in the eyes and one sees, by night the po lodges in the liver and one dreams.

src.l: various (Daoist); incl. 譚峭 Tan Qiao, 1576, 道宗六書 :6種, 36卷. [China] : 黄世厚, 明萬曆丙子 [4年, 1576].

src.l: various (Daoist); incl. 譚峭 Tan Qiao, 1576, 道宗六書 :6種, 36卷. [China] : 黄世厚, 明萬曆丙子 [4年, 1576].
src.q: During the day, the ethereal soul resides in the eyes; at night, the corporeal soul lodges in the liver.

s: Gao Lian's Zunsheng bajian (1591) gives a bedtime invocation to refine the three hun: the first hun guards the seven po, the second the Niwan (the head's elixir field), the third takes the heart's orders; bad dreams come when the seven po wander with the corpse-worms and ally with evil.

src.l: 高濂, 1596, 遵生八牋·卷九 (vol 7)

src.l: 高濂, 1596, 遵生八牋·卷九 (vol 7)
src.q: Let the first hun swiftly guard the seven po corporeal souls.
src.qo: 太洞真玄長練三魂第一魂速守七魄第二魂速守 泥丸第三魂受心節度

s: The Puji fang (1406) names the three hun, upper Shuangling 爽靈, middle Taiguang 胎光, lower Youjing 幽精; the hun want to rise to heaven and the po to sink into the springs; on the 3rd, 13th and 23rd of each month at evening the three hun leave the body and must be held back by a breathing and visualisation method.

src.loc: juan 264, citing 大微靈書; scan 113
src.q: 每月三日十三日二十三日夕三 魂離其身當須攝之

s: De Groot (1901) says the doctrine that a person has three hun and seven po, and five shen in the five viscera, comes from Daoist books, is 'not based on any teachings of the ancients', and was never a topic of the orthodox school.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1901, The Religious System of China, Vol. 4: The Soul in Philosophy and Folk-Conception
src.q: His hwun consists of three parts, and his pʻoh of seven, or — which comes to the same thing — he has three hwun and seven pʻoh. He possesses also five shen, each inhabiting one of his five viscera.

src.q: To say that "ghost" plus "cloud" forms the character for Hun, and "ghost" plus "white" forms the character for Po, is indeed so in the written script.

s: Critique: 'the soul' (Legge's 'soul and spirit', De Groot's 'dual soul', SL's rotating 'ethereal/spiritual/corporeal/physical/animal/bodily soul') presents hun and po as two halves of one entity, but the Chinese texts treat them as configurations of qi that part in opposite directions at death and disperse (Zhu Xi, Zhang Zai, the Liji); there is no single surviving subject for 'soul' to name.

s: Tertullian (De anima 9, c. 210) gives the soul the usual marks of a body, form, limitation and the three dimensions of length, breadth and height, and then a figure, against Plato, who denied the soul a figure lest it be composite and so dissoluble.

src.q: such as form³ and limitation; and that triad of dimensions⁴—I mean length, and breadth, and height—by which philosophers gauge all bodies. What now remains but for us to give the soul a figure?

s: Tertullian (De anima 9–10, c. 210) says the soul is in its material nature 'wind and breath' and that its figure is none other than the human form, the shape of the very body it animates, since God's breath passed through the face and spread through all the spaces of the body.

src.l: Tertullian, 1918, Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 3 (Tertullian), ed. Roberts & Donaldson

src.q: you can well imagine that it is none other than the human form; indeed, none other than the shape of that body which each individual soul animates and moves about.

s: Tertullian (De anima 27, c. 210), the founding text of traducianism, allows 'two kinds of seed', of the body and of the soul, but holds them inseparable and simultaneous in origin, so the soul is propagated with the body in the act of generation.

src.l: Tertullian, 1918, Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 3 (Tertullian), ed. Roberts & Donaldson

src.q: although we shall allow that there are two kinds of seed—that of the body and that of the soul—we still declare that they are inseparable, and therefore contemporaneous and simultaneous in origin.

s: Tertullian (De anima 5, c. 210) enlists the Stoics for the corporeal soul: Zeno's syllogism that what departs at death is a corporeal substance, and Cleanthes' argument that children resemble parents in soul as well as body.

src.l: Tertullian, 1918, Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 3 (Tertullian), ed. Roberts & Donaldson
src.loc: De anima 5 (Holmes's English, ANF 3 p.185); scan 199
src.q: But this spirit which is generated with (the body) is the soul: it follows, then, that the soul is a corporeal substance.

s: Claudianus Mamertus (De statu animae, c. 469) finds 'traces of numbers' (uestigia numerorum) in every body in three ways: it is one, it has parts, and every part is again one divisible body 'because of the primordial power of number'; the soul's greatness is not so measured.

s: Claudianus Mamertus (De statu animae, c. 469) answers Faustus' dilemma (everywhere or nowhere) by analogy: as God is whole everywhere in the universe, the soul is whole everywhere in the body, not in a part of the body by a part of itself.

src.l: Claudianus Mamertus, August Engelbrecht (ed.), 1885, Claudiani Mamerti Opera (CSEL XI)
src.q: just as God is everywhere whole in the universe, so this [the soul] is found everywhere whole in the body.

s: Augustine (De quantitate animae, 388; Latin printed 1472) answers Evodius' question 'how great is the soul?' by distinguishing spatial size from power, and affirms that the soul is 'not long, nor wide, nor robust, nor any of those things which are wont to be sought in the measures of bodies'.

src.q: I can affirm this: that it is not long, nor wide, nor robust, nor any of those things which are wont to be sought in the measures of bodies.
src.qo: Nō enī vllo mō aut longa aut lata aut quasi valida suspicanda est aia.

src.q: Nō enī vllo mō aut longa aut lata aut quasi valida suspicanda est aia.

s: Augustine (De Trinitate X.10, c. 417) argues that the mind knows with certainty that it is, lives and understands, but is not certain whether it is air, fire or any body; since knowing itself it knows its substance, it is in no way a body.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1489, De Trinitate
src.q: Nor is it certain at all whether it is air or fire, or some body, or something corporeal. Therefore, it is in no way some body.
src.qo: omnis enim se intelligere nouerit et esse et viuere.

s: Augustine (De Trinitate, c. 417; recapitulation in book XV) says book X found 'a still more manifest trinity of the mind' in memory, understanding and will, after book IX's trinity of mind, its self-knowledge and its self-love.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1489, De Trinitate
src.q: we found in the mind a still more manifest trinity of the mind, viz. in memory, and understanding, and will

s: Augustine (Retractationes II, 427; English 1968) records that he had confessed he did not know whether souls are propagated from the first man and then from parents or given to each without propagation, but that he certainly knew 'the soul is not body, but spirit', and that he defended this 'hesitation' against Vincentius Victor.

src.q: I defended my hesitation concerning the origin of the souls which are given to individual men

s: An excerpt 'from Augustine On the origin of the soul' printed in a 1475 Augustine volume says: concerning my soul, I do not know how it came into my body; He who gave it knows whether He drew it from my father or created a new one, and I am not ashamed to confess that I do not know what I do not know.

src.q: I say concerning my soul, I do not know how it came into my body; for I did not bestow it upon myself. He knows who bestowed it, whether He drew it from my father or whether He created a new one for the first man.

s: Agrippa (De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum, 1530; ed. 1598) reports a 'dissension' among Christian theologians on the origin of souls: Origen held all souls made in heaven at the world's origin; Augustine thought the first man's soul came from heaven, older than the body, though 'he does not seem to affirm even this with sufficient consistency'.

s: Nemesius of Emesa (De natura hominis, c. 390) localises the inner faculties in the brain's ventricles: the anterior ventricles are the roots of the senses (with imagination), the middle belongs to thinking, the posterior (cerebellum) to memory, with the 'psychic pneuma' in it.

s: Nemesius (De natura hominis 2, c. 390) refutes the soul as temperament (krasis) of the body: a temperament changes with diet and seasons, so we would not keep the same soul; and temperament cooperates with the body's desires, while the soul opposes them.

src.q: Furthermore, the temperament does not oppose the desires of the body, but rather cooperates with them, for it is the temperament that initiates the movement. The soul, however, does oppose these desires. Therefore, the temperament is not the soul.

s: Nemesius (De natura hominis 2, c. 390) concludes that, having shown the soul is neither a body, nor a harmony, nor a mixture, nor any other quality, it is an incorporeal substance, since all agree it exists.

s: Aquinas (Summa theologiae I q.75 a.1, c. 1266) argues that no body is a principle of life just because it is a body, so the soul, 'the first principle of life', is not a body but the act of a body, as heat is the principle of heating.

s: Aquinas (ST I q.76 a.1, c. 1266) holds that the intellect, the principle of intellectual operation, is the form of the human body, because that by which something primarily operates is the form of that to which the operation is attributed; against making it only a mover, 'it is not because Socrates is moved by the intellect that he understands'.

s: Critique: on SL's pages 'soul' is not a stable rendering even of one word. Homer's psychē is 'souls', 'life' and 'spirit' within the Loeb Iliad (twice on one page), Hartmann's Seele is 'soul' while seelisch is 'mental', Hegel's Geist is 'Spirit' in one SL book and 'Mind' in another, nefesh is 'persons', 'life', 'living soul' and (wrongly) 'soul' for a word that can name a corpse. s: Critique: reading Homer's psychē as 'the soul' inverts the Homeric person. Iliad I.3-4 sets the psychai sent to Hades against the heroes 'themselves' left to the dogs, and Odyssey XI's psychē is an untouchable image; the self is the body, the psychē what leaves it. The inversion is old (the pseudo-Plutarchan Life of Homer makes the same flight-to-Hades line proof of the immortal soul) and survives in SL's English, which drops 'themselves'.

s: Critique: Budge's English puts Christian diction on the Egyptian ba: a section headed 'The Doctrine of Eternal Life', 'Holy Soul' and 'soul of God' for ba of gods, 'thy soul is to heaven'. The Egyptian texts give the ba a place among the gods and a return to the body (Book of the Dead 89, 91), not salvation from it; SL's model then adds 'personality or soul' to Budge's 'heart-soul (Ba)'.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1913, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani
src.q: The Doctrine of Eternal Life

s: Critique: 'the soul' presumes one per person, but the pages hold plural systems in nearly every tradition: Egyptian ba, akh, ka, khaba; hun and po; nefesh, ruach, neshamah; Greenlanders' shadow and breath; Dakota, Nahua and Yoruba several souls; and in French Christianity Saint-Martin's âme de sang beside the intelligent soul. Tylor lists most of them and files them as speculation from 'the savage condition'; De Groot and Legge fold hun and po into one soul.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: Suffice it to point out here that such speculation dates back to the savage condition of our race

src.l: Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin, 1807, Oeuvres posthumes
src.q: il faut croire que cette âme animale n'est autre chose que l'âme de sang

s: Critique: Tylor's 'doctrine of souls' (1871) is a theory, not a finding: it derives every soul word from breath, shadow and dream, orders the doctrines from savage to cultured, and reads a two-soul system as vagueness. The outsider sources of the world-* thread (Ellis, Skeat, Best, Tregear, Spencer and Gillen, Budge) write in its vocabulary, 'spirit or living principle', 'vital principle', 'double', so their glosses carry the frame into the catalogue.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: Let us see at a glance in what general relation the doctrine of souls among savage tribes stands to the doctrine of souls among barbaric and cultured nations.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: how loose and vague such ideas are among the lower races

s: Critique: Tylor's breath-word table (nephesh, ruach, nefs, ātman, psychē, anima all 'breath') is good etymology and bad conceptual history. On SL's own pages the words have left breath behind in different directions: nefesh counts persons (Exodus), psychē is a man's 'life' (Iliad IX), nafs is the source of evil (Hujwiri), ātman is Brahman (Chāndogya). A common origin does not make a common concept.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: The same is the history of Sanskrit âtman and prâna, of Greek psychē and pneuma, of Latin animus, anima, spiritus.

s: Critique: Spencer's ghost theory and Frazer's external soul finish Tylor's frame. Spencer makes the soul a 'double' the savage infers because he cannot tell sleep and swoon from death; Frazer makes it a life the savage cannot think abstractly and so lodges in an object. Both explain a belief by an error of the believer, which is why neither can tell a Dakota nagi from a Nahua tonalli: the theory needs only the error.

src.l: Herbert Spencer, 1897, The Principles of Sociology, Vol. I (3rd ed.)
src.loc: Preface to the third edition, p. viii; scan 5
src.q: I discovered no attempt to deal with the hypothesis that religion is evolved from the ghost-theory

s: Critique: the flattening is not only a problem of far languages. Descartes calls the thinking thing esprit and âme on one page, rendered 'mind' and 'soul'; Hartmann's Seele and seelisch become 'soul' and 'mental'; Hegel's Geist is 'Spirit' or 'Mind' by translator. English forces a choice among soul, spirit and mind that French and German do not make, so q:soul-mind-spirit-life answers partly reflect the English.

src.l: René Descartes, 1637, Discours de la Methode
src.q: Car ce n'est pas assez d'auoir l'esprit bon, mais le principal est de l'appliquer bien. Les plus grandes ames sont capables des plus grans vices

s: Critique: edition date is not work date, and the dates in the tooling show it. In the census 537 of 1293 live soul books are dated by author lifespan and 737 by model knowledge; Tylor's Primitive Culture II gets 1882 (work 1871, SL copy 1920), Hartmann 1863 (work 1869), Budge's Book of the Dead text 1891; aliveness-kb's sources date Tylor I to 1859 and Descartes' Discourse to 1624 (work 1637). SL's 'The Principles of Psychology' (Spencer, 1897), dated 1855, is in fact the Principles of Sociology (1876).

src.q: ANCESTOR-WORSHIP IN GENERAL

s: Critique: the shelf leans. Of 1293 live soul books (537 translated), 519 are Latin (40.1%), 429 English, 187 German and 51 French (91.7% together); Greek 23, Hebrew 15, Chinese 15, Egyptian 11, Tibetan 1, and no live Arabic, Sanskrit or Pali book. By work date, 451 are 16th-17th century and 451 19th-20th (34.9% each), 98 before 500 CE. Counts of 'what traditions said' measure the library.

src.l: soul-kb, 2026, Soul shelf census of Source Library (research/shelf-2026-10-26.json)

s: Descartes (Passions of the Soul I.30, 1649; Latin 1650) holds that the soul is truly joined to the whole body and cannot properly be said to be in any one part of it to the exclusion of the others, because the body is one and in a way indivisible by the disposition of its organs.

src.l: René Descartes, 1650, Passiones animae (Latin translation of Les passions de l'âme)
src.q: it is necessary to know that the soul is truly joined to the whole body, and that it cannot properly be said to be in any one part of it, to the exclusion of the others
src.qo: oportet scire animam esse re- vera junctam toti corpori, nec posse proprie dici eam esse in quadam parte ejus, exclusivè ad alias

src.l: René Descartes, 1650, Passiones animae (Latin translation of Les passions de l'âme)
src.q: oportet scire animam esse re- vera junctam toti corpori, nec posse proprie dici eam esse in quadam parte ejus, exclusivè ad alias

s: Descartes (Passions I.30, Latin 1650) argues that the soul has no relation to extension or dimensions but only to the whole complex of the organs: a half or a third of a soul cannot be conceived, it does not shrink when a limb is cut off, and it leaves whole when the organs' assembly is dissolved.

src.l: René Descartes, 1650, Passiones animae (Latin translation of Les passions de l'âme)
src.q: a half or a third part of the soul can in no way be conceived, nor what extension it occupies
src.qo: quod animæ dimidia vel tertia pars nullo modo concipi possit, aut quam extensionem occupet

src.l: René Descartes, 1650, Passiones animae (Latin translation of Les passions de l'âme)
src.q: quod animæ dimidia vel tertia pars nullo modo concipi possit, aut quam extensionem occupet

s: Descartes (Passions I.31, Latin 1650) heads the article: there is a gland in the brain in which the soul exercises its functions more particularly than in the other parts, although it is joined to the whole body.

src.l: René Descartes, 1650, Passiones animae (Latin translation of Les passions de l'âme)
src.q: That there is a gland in the brain, in which the soul exercises its functions more particularly than in the other parts.
src.qo: Dari glandulam in cerebro, in qua anima suas functiones specialius quam in aliis partibus exerceat.

src.l: René Descartes, 1650, Passiones animae (Latin translation of Les passions de l'âme)
src.q: Dari glandulam in cerebro, in qua anima suas functiones specialius quam in aliis partibus exerceat.

s: Descartes (Passions I.32, 1649; Haldane-Ross English 1911) gives his reason the gland is the soul's main seat: every other part of the brain is double, as are the eyes, hands and ears, while thought is one.

src.l: René Descartes, Elizabeth S. Haldane, G. R. T. Ross, 1912, The Philosophical Works of Descartes, Vol. I (Haldane-Ross translation)
src.q: The reason which persuades me that the soul cannot have any other seat in all the body than this gland wherein to exercise its functions immediately, is that I reflect that the other parts of our brain are all of them double

s: Descartes (Meditations VI, 1641) says nature teaches him he is not in his body as a sailor in a ship but very closely joined and as it were intermingled with it, so that he and the body make one thing; otherwise, being only a thinking thing, he would perceive an injury by pure intellect, not feel pain.

src.l: René Descartes, 1641, Meditationes de prima philosophia
src.q: Nature teaches me that I am not merely present in my body as a sailor is present in a ship . Instead, I am very closely joined to it and, as it were, intermingled with it, so much so that I and the body form a single unit.
src.qo: me non tantùm adesse meo corpori vt nauta adest na- uigio, sed illi arctissimè esse coniun- ctum, & quasi permixtum, adeò vt vnum quid cum illo componam

src.l: René Descartes, 1641, Meditationes de prima philosophia
src.q: me non tantùm adesse meo corpori vt nauta adest na- uigio, sed illi arctissimè esse coniun- ctum, & quasi permixtum, adeò vt vnum quid cum illo componam

s: Gassendi (Fifth Objections to the Meditations, 1641) protests that when Descartes concludes he is precisely 'a thinking thing, that is, mens, sive animus, intellectus, ratio', Gassendi had thought he was addressing the human soul (anima), the inner principle by which a man lives, senses, moves and understands, and finds he was addressing only the mind.

src.l: René Descartes, 1641, Meditationes de prima philosophia
src.loc: Objectiones Quintae (Gassendi) on Med. II; scan 397 (SL English)
src.q: I thought I was addressing the human soul —that internal principle by which a human being lives, senses, moves from place to place, and understands. Instead, I find I was addressing only the mind .
src.qo: Existimabam enim me alloqui animam humanam, seu internũ illud principium, quo homo viuit, sentit, loco mouetur, intelligit: & alloquebar tamen solã mentem

src.l: René Descartes, 1641, Meditationes de prima philosophia
src.q: Existimabam enim me alloqui animam humanam, seu internũ illud principium, quo homo viuit, sentit, loco mouetur, intelligit: & alloquebar tamen solã mentem

s: Henry More (The Immortality of the Soul III, 1659; Collection 1662) holds that the soul considered in its own essence, without reference to any body, is 'a Substance extended and indiscerpible': extended like body, but not able to be torn apart.

src.l: Henry More, 1662, A Collection of Several Philosophical Writings of Dr. Henry More
src.loc: Immortality of the Soul, III.1 ('the Soul out of the Body'); scan 537
src.q: we shall find her a Substance extended and indiscerpible

s: Henry More (Collection of Philosophical Writings, 1662) names a fourth mode of spiritual substance beside the three dimensions, 'Essential Spissitude', the power of a substance to receive one part of itself into another, so that what is lost in extension is kept in thickness.

src.l: Henry More, 1662, A Collection of Several Philosophical Writings of Dr. Henry More
src.loc: Preface to The Immortality of the Soul (scan 406)
src.q: is kept safe in Essential Spissitude: For so I will call this Mode or Property of a Substance, that is able to receive one part of it self into another.

s: Henry More (Preface, 1662) argues that what a phantasm is to our soul a fabric is to the Spirit of Nature: as the tenor of our spirits, 'but subtile matter', makes the soul exert itself into an imagination without premeditation, so a disposition of the world's matter makes the Spirit of Nature fall on an organisation without perception.

src.l: Henry More, 1662, A Collection of Several Philosophical Writings of Dr. Henry More
src.q: what Phantasme is to our Soul, that Fabrick is to the Spirit of Nature

s: Cudworth (True Intellectual System, 1678) states the grand objection to making sensitive as well as rational souls substances: it would follow that the souls of brutes subsist after the animals' deaths, which seems absurd to two sorts of men.

src.l: Ralph Cudworth, 1678, The true intellectual system of the universe: the first part; wherein, all the reason and philosophy of atheism is confuted; and its impossibility demonstrated. By R. Cudworth, D.D.
src.q: The Grand Objection against this Substantiality of Souls Sensitive, as well as Rational, is from that Consequence, which will be from thence inferred, of their Permanent Subsistence after Death

s: Spinoza (Ethics II P13, 1677) holds that the object of the idea constituting the human mind is the body, a certain mode of extension actually existing, and nothing else.

src.l: Baruch Spinoza, 1915, Ethica (Latin original)
src.q: The object of the idea constituting the human Mind is the Body, or a certain mode of Extension actually existing, and nothing else.
src.qo: Objectum ideæ humanam Mentem constituentis est Corpus, sive certus Extensionis modus actu existens, et nihil aliud.

src.l: Baruch Spinoza, 1915, Ethica (Latin original)
src.q: Objectum ideæ humanam Mentem constituentis est Corpus, sive certus Extensionis modus actu existens, et nihil aliud.

s: Spinoza (Ethics V P23, 1677) holds that the human mind cannot be absolutely destroyed with the body, but something of it remains which is eternal, because in God there is an idea expressing the essence of this body under a kind of eternity.

src.l: Baruch Spinoza, 1915, Ethica (Latin original)
src.q: The human Mind cannot be absolutely destroyed with the Body, but something of it remains which is eternal.
src.qo: Mens humana non potest cum Corpore absolute destrui, sed ejus aliquid remanet, quod æternum est.

src.l: Baruch Spinoza, 1915, Ethica (Latin original)
src.q: Mens humana non potest cum Corpore absolute destrui, sed ejus aliquid remanet, quod æternum est.

s: Leibniz (Théodicée, 1710) argues that as divine preformation made the admirable automata of nature that produce the fetus mechanically, so the soul is a spiritual automaton, still more admirable, producing by divine preformation ideas in which our will has no part.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1714, Essais de théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu, la liberté de l'homme et l'origine du mal
src.q: it is easy to judge in the same way that the soul is a spiritual automaton, even more admirable; and that it is by divine preformation that it produces these beautiful ideas
src.qo: il est aisé de juger de même que l'ame est un automate spirituel, encore plus admirable; & que c'est par la préformation divine qu'elle produit ces belles idées

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1714, Essais de théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu, la liberté de l'homme et l'origine du mal
src.q: il est aisé de juger de même que l'ame est un automate spirituel, encore plus admirable; & que c'est par la préformation divine qu'elle produit ces belles idées

s: Leibniz (remarks on Wachter, the 'Refutation of Spinoza', c. 1707-10) says the soul, and the mind no less, acts spontaneously and yet like a spiritual automaton: as in bodies everything is done by motions under the laws of force, so in the soul by effort or desire under the laws of the Good, and the two realms are in harmony.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1840, Philosophical Works (Monadology, Theodicy, Letters to Clarke), English
src.q: I say that the soul acts spontaneously and yet like a spiritual automaton; and that this is true also of the mind.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1840, Philosophical Works (Monadology, Theodicy, Letters to Clarke), English
src.q: as in bodies everything is done by motions according to the laws of force, so in the soul everything is done through effort or desire, according to the laws of the Good. The two realms are in harmony.

s: Latta's note to the Monadology (1898) traces the phrase 'spiritual automaton' to Spinoza, who in the Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect (§85) speaks of the soul acting according to certain laws 'as if it were a kind of spiritual automaton'.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Robert Latta (tr., ed.), 1898, The Monadology and Other Philosophical Writings, tr. Robert Latta (Oxford, 1898)
src.loc: Latta's note to the Monadology; scan 249
src.q: Spinoza speaks of the soul as ‘acting according to certain laws and as if it were a kind of spiritual automaton.’ De Intellectus Emendatione, 85

s: In the notes to Locke's Essay (1710 ed., II.27), Locke quotes Bishop Stillingfleet: the resurrected body is the same 'Not from the Consciousness of the Soul, but from that Life which is the Result of the Union of the Soul and Body'.

src.l: John Locke, 1710, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Vol. 1 (6th ed., with the Stillingfleet replies as notes)
src.q: Not from the Consciousness of the Soul, but from that Life which is the Result of the Union of the Soul and Body.

s: In his reply to Stillingfleet printed with the 1710 Essay, Locke says that if God gave a system of very subtle matter sense and motion, it might with propriety of speech be called spirit, materiality not being excluded from its complex idea.

src.l: John Locke, 1710, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Vol. 2
src.q: it might, with propriety of Speech, be called Spirit

s: Leibniz (Nouveaux essais II.27, written 1703-05), answering Locke, holds that if God changed a man's real identity his personal identity would remain so long as the appearances of identity were kept, inner (consciousness) and outer (how he appears to others): consciousness is not the only way to constitute personal identity.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1965, Die philosophischen Schriften (Gerhardt), SL 'Vol. 3' (Nouveaux essais, 'Leibniz und Locke')
src.q: Thus, consciousness is not the only means of establishing personal identity, and the reports of others or even other signs can supplement it.
src.qo: Ainsi la conscience n'est pas le seul moyen de constituer l'identité personelle, et le rapport d'autruy ou mêmes d'autres marques y peuvent suppléer

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1965, Die philosophischen Schriften (Gerhardt), SL 'Vol. 3' (Nouveaux essais, 'Leibniz und Locke')
src.q: Ainsi la conscience n'est pas le seul moyen de constituer l'identité personelle, et le rapport d'autruy ou mêmes d'autres marques y peuvent suppléer

s: Thomas Willis (De anima brutorum, 1672) compares the corporeal soul, the soul of brutes, with the rational soul, and announces three heads: that the rational far excels the brutal, how both souls are joined in man, and how they often disagree.

src.l: Thomas Willis, 1672, De anima brutorum
src.loc: Cap. VII heading and margin; scan 180 (SL English)
src.q: The corporeal soul, or the soul of animals, is compared with the rational soul. … How both souls are joined in a human.
src.qo: Anima corporea, sive Brutorum, cum Anima rationali comparatur. … Quomodo utræque animæ in homine conjunguntur

src.l: Thomas Willis, 1672, De anima brutorum
src.q: Anima corporea, sive Brutorum, cum Anima rationali comparatur. … Quomodo utræque animæ in homine conjunguntur

s: Girolamo Rorario's dialogue, written in the 1540s and printed 1648, is titled 'That brute animals often use reason better than man' (Quod animalia bruta saepe ratione utantur melius homine).

src.l: Girolamo Rorario (Hieronymus Rorarius), 1648, Quod animalia bruta ratione utantur melius homine libri duo
src.loc: Liber primus, title; scan 19 (Latin; no SL translation)
src.q: QVOD ANIMALIA BRVTA Saepe ratione utantur meliùs Homine.

s: Carr's commentary on the Monadology (1930) reports that Bayle's Dictionary article 'Rorarius', whose notes fill twelve folio columns, is referred to and answered in the Monadology, and that Rorarius's book argued that the brutes have a rational soul and use reason better than men.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1930, The Monadology of Leibniz (English translation with commentary)
src.q: Bayle’s article “Rorarius”, which is referred to and replied to in the Monadology, derives its whole interest from its application to the doctrine of Leibniz.

s: Joseph Glanvill (Lux orientalis, 1662) defends the pre-existence of souls, 'that our souls were extant before these earthly bodies', and says the objections prove only that objectors cannot conceive what the pre-existent state was.

src.l: Joseph Glanvill, 1662, Lux orientalis, or an enquiry into the opinion of the eastern sages concerning the praeexistence of souls
src.q: that our souls were extant before these earthly bodies

s: Swedenborg (Heaven and Hell, 1758; English 1875) holds that while man is in the natural world he is in a terrestrial body, and when he leaves it he enters the spiritual world and puts on a spiritual body, in perfect human form like the angels.

src.l: Emanuel Swedenborg, 1875, Heaven and Its Wonders and Hell (English, 1875 ed.)
src.loc: n. 485 (before n. 486 on the scan); scan 341
src.q: so long as man is in the natural world he is in a terrestrial body ; but when he leaves that body he enters the spiritual world and puts on a spiritual body.

s: Swedenborg (Rational Psychology, written 1742; English 1900) distinguishes a superior mind and an inferior mind 'or mind properly so called', both reigning in the animated body, and places the soul's life so deep within that it is distant from the animus by several degrees of perfection.

src.l: Emanuel Swedenborg, 1900, The Soul, or Rational Psychology (English tr. of Psychologia rationalis)
src.q: There are therefore a superior mind and an inferior mind (or mind properly so called)

src.l: Emanuel Swedenborg, 1900, The Soul, or Rational Psychology (English tr. of Psychologia rationalis)
src.q: distant from the animus by several degrees of perfection

s: Swedenborg (Rational Psychology, 1742; English 1900) says sensations climb from the outermost to the innermost and actions descend, and that the cortical brain holds the inmost and highest place.

src.l: Emanuel Swedenborg, 1900, The Soul, or Rational Psychology (English tr. of Psychologia rationalis)
src.q: The cortical brain holds the inmost and the highest

s: Willis (De anima brutorum VII, 1672) makes the rational soul's priority lie in its objects: every corporeal faculty is limited to sensible things of one kind, while the object of the human mind is all being, material or immaterial, real or fictional.

src.l: Thomas Willis, 1672, De anima brutorum
src.q: every corporeal faculty is limited to sensible things. Each one is restricted to a certain kind of thing. In contrast, the object of the human mind is all being.

s: Against 'Descartes put the soul in the pineal gland': in the Passions he first says the soul is joined to the whole body and has no relation to extension or dimensions (I.30), and calls the gland the place where it exercises its functions more particularly (I.31); the gland is where soul and body interact, not where the soul is contained.

src.l: René Descartes, 1650, Passiones animae (Latin translation of Les passions de l'âme)
src.q: the soul is of such a nature that it has no relation to extension, or dimensions, or other properties of the matter of which the body consists

s: Joseph Butler (Dissertation 'Of Personal Identity', 1736) objects to Locke that consciousness of personal identity presupposes, and so cannot constitute, personal identity, as knowledge cannot constitute the truth it presupposes.

src.l: Joseph Butler, 1736, The Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed (Dissertation I, Of Personal Identity)
src.q: Consciousness of personal Identity presupposes, and therefore cannot constitute, personal Identity; any more than Knowledge, in any other Case, can constitute Truth, which it presupposes.

s: Agrippa (De occulta philosophia III.43, 1533) calls the 'idol' of the soul the life-giving and governing power of the body and the origin of the senses, through which the soul unfolds sensing in the body; it is the knot of body and soul, below fate and above the body.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres (1533)
src.q: I call the idol of the soul that life-giving and governing power of the body, the origin of the senses, through which the soul itself unfolds the powers of sensing in this body.

s: Agrippa (III.43) holds that nothing in mind, idolum, nature or body passes into the soul unless reason turns toward it: the soul does not perceive itself to see or hear until thinking reason grasps it, as people lost in thought fail to notice those who meet them.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres (1533)
src.q: cannot pass into the soul unless reason intends itself toward it. In this way, in the external senses, the soul perceives itself neither to see, nor hear, nor sense, nor suffer anything, until the thinking reason first grasps it.
src.qo: Hoc modo in ſenſibus exterioribus anima nec uidere, nec audire, nec ſentire, nec pati ſe quicq̄ percipit, donec ratio cogitatrix id prius comprehendat:

s: Agrippa (III.44) makes the mind immortal and reason long-lived, but the idolum, the sensible and animal soul drawn from corporeal matter, perishes with the body or lingers briefly as a shade in its vapours.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres (1533)
src.q: the sensible and animal soul itself, because it was drawn from the lap of corporeal matter, perishes along with the body when it is dissolved.

s: Budge's 1898 Book of the Dead introduction divides the person into a perishable material body (khat), preserved only by mummifying, and a sāḥu that grows from it after the rites and ascends to the gods, for which he says the 'only suitable rendering' is 'spiritual body'.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1898, The Book of the Dead: The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day (English translation, with introduction)
src.loc: Introduction, 'component parts of man's entity', scan 120
src.q: The physical or material body, called khat, was liable to decay, and could only be preserved by mummifying

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1898, The Book of the Dead: The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day (English translation, with introduction)
src.q: The only suitable ren- dering for the word sāḥu is "spiritual body"

s: Budge (1898) says ka is 'now generally rendered by "double"', glosses it with Coptic κω and Greek εἴδωλον, and calls it an 'abstract individuality or personality' that lives in the tomb, wanders at will and can go and dwell in a man's statue.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1898, The Book of the Dead: The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day (English translation, with introduction)
src.q: it is now generally rendered by "double" ; it has its equivalent in the Coptic κω and in the Greek εἴδωλον

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1898, The Book of the Dead: The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day (English translation, with introduction)
src.q: This abstract individuality or personality possessed all the attributes of the man himself, and, though its normal dwelling- place was in the tomb along with the body, it could wander about at will

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1898, The Book of the Dead: The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day (English translation, with introduction)
src.q: it was independent of the man to whom it belonged and could even go and dwell in the statue of a man

s: Budge (1898) renders ba simply 'soul' and reports two strands: in some texts it eats the funeral offerings with the ka, in others it ascends to heaven to live with Rā and the beatified dead.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1898, The Book of the Dead: The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day (English translation, with introduction)
src.q: Connected in some inexplicable way with the ka was the ba, or soul, which according to some texts is said to eat of the funeral offerings along with the ka, in whom or with whom it was supposed to dwell, but according to others it ascended into heaven where it lived with Rā and the beatified dead

s: Budge (1898) says the ba could leave heaven and visit the body whenever it pleased and 'had power to assume any form which it pleased'.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1898, The Book of the Dead: The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day (English translation, with introduction)
src.q: The ba could leave its place in heaven and visit the body whenever it pleased, and it had power to assume any form which it pleased

s: Budge (1898) says the heart (ab) shared characteristics of the ba and 'was believed to be the source both of life and of good and evil in man', which is why several chapters guard it.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1898, The Book of the Dead: The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day (English translation, with introduction)

s: Budge (1913) says the BA, 'which beyond all doubt was believed to enjoy an eternal existence', has 'always hitherto been translated by "soul," or "heart-soul"', is drawn as a human-headed hawk and is 'exceedingly refined or ethereal' in substance.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1913, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani
src.q: To that part of man which beyond all doubt was believed to enjoy an eternal existence after the death of the body, the Egyptians gave the name BA , a word which has been thought to mean something like "sublime," "noble," and which has always hitherto been translated by "soul," or "heart-soul."

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1913, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani
src.q: In form it is depicted as a human-headed hawk , and in nature and substance it is stated to be exceedingly refined or ethereal

s: Budge (1913) defines KHU as a 'shining' or translucent Spirit-soul and says that though it 'has often been translated "shining one," "glorious," "intelligence,"' its 'true meaning must be Spirit-soul'.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1913, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani
src.q: Another important and apparently eternal part of man was the KHU, 𓅼, which, judging from the meaning of the word, may be defined as a " shining " or translucent Spirit-soul. For want of a better word KHU has often been translated " shining one," " glorious," " intelligence," and the like, but its true meaning must be Spirit-soul

s: Budge (1913) compares the KHAIBIT, the shadow 'which the Egyptians regarded as a part of the human economy', with the σκιά and umbra of the Greeks and Romans.

src.q: In connection with the KA and BA must be mentioned the KHAIBIT, , or shadow of the man, which the Egyptians regarded as a part of the human economy. It may be compared with the σκιά and umbra of the Greeks and Romans

s: Budge (1913) sums up that 'the whole man consisted of a natural body, a Spirit-body, a heart, a double, a Heart-soul, a shadow, a Spirit-soul, and a name', all 'bound together inseparably', so that the welfare of each concerned all.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1913, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani
src.q: Thus, as we have seen, the whole man consisted of a natural body, a Spirit-body, a heart, a double, a Heart-soul, a shadow, a Spirit-soul, and a name. All these were, however, bound together inseparably, and the welfare of any single one of them concerned the welfare of all

s: Herodotus (Histories II.123, c. 430 BCE) reports the Egyptian doctrine that the human soul (ψυχή) is immortal and, when the body perishes, enters another creature being born, passing through all land, sea and air creatures back into a human body in 3,000 years, and that some Greeks took it as their own.

src.l: Herodotus, 1884, Herodoti Historiae (Greek, with SL English)
src.q: ὡς ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴ ἀθάνατος ἐστί, τοῦ σώματος δὲ κα- ταφθίνοντος ἐς ἄλλο ζῷον αἰεὶ γινόμενον ἐσδύεται, ἐπεὰν δὲ πάντα περιέλθῃ τὰ χερσαῖα καὶ τὰ θαλάσσια καὶ τὰ πετεινά, αὖτις ἐς ἀνθρώπου σῶμα γινόμενον ἐσδύειν· τὴν 5 περιήλυσιν δὲ αὐτῇ γίνεσθαι ἐν τρισχιλίοισι ἔτεσι.

src.l: Herodotus, 1884, Herodoti Historiae (Greek, with SL English)
src.q: that the soul of man is immortal. When the body dies, it enters into another living creature as it is being born. When it has traveled through all the creatures of the land, the sea, and the air, it enters once more into the body of a human being at birth. This cycle is completed in three thousand years.

s: Aristotle opens his review of earlier views of soul (De anima I.2, 403b25-27, c. 350 BCE) by saying that his predecessors fixed on two marks of what has soul as against what has not: movement and sensation.

s: Aristotle (De anima I.2, 404a1-9) reports that Democritus made soul a sort of fire or hot substance: of the infinitely many atoms, the spherical ones are fire and soul, like the motes seen in sunbeams, chosen because that shape best permeates everything and moves the rest.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)

s: Aristotle (De anima I.2, 404a9-16) adds that for Democritus breathing is what keeps a creature alive: the restless soul-atoms would be squeezed out by the surrounding air, so similar atoms drawn in by respiration reinforce them, and animals live only as long as they can maintain this resistance.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)

s: Aristotle (De anima I.2, 404a27-31) says Democritus 'roundly identifies soul and mind', because he identifies what appears with what is true, and so does not treat mind as a special faculty dealing with truth; Anaxagoras is more obscure.

s: Aristotle (De anima I.2, 405b1-8) reports that Hippo made the soul water, arguing from the fluid seed, and that Critias and others made it blood, because they took perception to be the most characteristic attribute of soul and traced perception to the blood.

s: The Stoics (Diogenes Laertius VII.156-157) make the soul the pneuma connate with us, hence a body that survives death but is perishable, while the soul of the whole, of which ours are parts, is imperishable; Zeno, Antipater and Posidonius call it warm pneuma; Cleanthes has all souls last until the conflagration, Chrysippus only the souls of the wise.

src.l: Diogenes Laertius, R. D. Hicks (tr.), 1925, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Vol. 2 (Loeb)
src.q: And they regard it as the breath of life, congenital with us; from which they infer first that it is a body and secondly that it survives death. Yet it is perishable

src.l: Diogenes Laertius, R. D. Hicks (tr.), 1925, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Vol. 2 (Loeb)
src.q: Cleanthes indeed holds that all souls continue to exist until the general conflagration; but Chrysippus says that only the souls of the wise do so.

src.l: Diogenes Laertius, R. D. Hicks (tr.), 1925, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Vol. 2 (Loeb)
src.q: ταύτην δ’ εἶναι τὸ συμφυὲς ἡμῖν πνεῦμα· διὸ καὶ σῶμα εἶναι καὶ μετὰ τὸν θάνατον ἐπιμένειν· φθαρτὴν δ’ ὑπάρχειν

src.l: Diogenes Laertius, R. D. Hicks (tr.), 1925, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Vol. 2 (Loeb)
src.q: Κλεάνθης μὲν οὖν πάσας ἐπιδιαμένειν μέχρι τῆς ἐκπυρώσεως, Χρύσιππος δὲ τὰς τῶν σοφῶν μόνον

s: The Stoics (DL VII.157) count eight parts of the soul: the five senses, the seminal principles in us, the vocal part and the reasoning part.

src.l: Diogenes Laertius, R. D. Hicks (tr.), 1925, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Vol. 2 (Loeb)
src.q: They count eight parts of the soul: the five senses, the generative power in us, our power of speech, and that of reasoning.

s: Chrysippus (On the Soul I, quoted by Galen, SVF II.894 and 896, 3rd c. BCE) locates the ruling part (hēgemonikon) of the soul in the heart: speech (logos) and thought have one source, and these are manifestly about the heart, sent from it through the throat; even the name kardia comes from the ruling, mastering (kratēsis) part of the soul in it.

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippus
src.q: These things occur manifestly around the heart, being sent forth from the heart through the throat and the voice
src.qo: ταῦτα δὲ ἐκφανῶς περὶ τὴν καρδίαν γίγνεται, ἐκ τῆς καρδίας διὰ φάρυγγος καὶ τῆς φωνῆς καὶ τοῦ λόγου ἐκπεμπομένων.

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippus
src.q: the heart has also obtained this name by a certain ruling and lordship, from the fact that the part of the soul that rules and holds sway is in it
src.qo: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐν αὐτῇ εἶναι τὸ κυριεῦον καὶ κρατοῦν τῆς ψυχῆς μέρος, ὡς ἂν κρατία λεγομένη

s: Aristotle's strongest objection to the self-moving number (De anima I.4, 409a1-b18): if psychic units move they trace lines, so the soul's number must have position; plants and many animals live on when cut, but a number minus a unit is a different number; and units with position are just Democritus' spherical atoms shrunk to points, so the number-soul is atomism in disguise.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: the movements of the psychic units must be lines (for a point is a unit having position, and the number of the soul is, of course, somewhere and has position)

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: if from a number a number or a unit is subtracted, the remainder is another number; but plants and many animals when divided continue to live

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: It must be all the same whether we speak of units or corpuscles; for if the spherical atoms of Democritus became points, nothing being retained but their being a quantum

s: Aristotle (De anima I.3, 407b20-26) objects to the Pythagorean myths that any soul could be clothed in any body: each body has its own form and shape, and it is as absurd as saying carpentry could embody itself in flutes; each art must use its own tools, each soul its body.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: as in the Pythagorean myths, that any soul could be clothed upon with any body—an absurd view, for each body seems to have a form and shape of its own

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: It is as absurd as to say that the art of carpentry could embody itself in flutes; each art must use its tools, each soul its body.

s: The self-moving-number definition is backdated in the doxography: Aristotle gives it to unnamed 'thinkers' (404b27), Plutarch to Xenocrates (1012d), but Aëtius (IV.2) heads it with Pythagoras and makes Xenocrates his follower; the oldest witness does not support a Pythagorean origin.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: have compounded it of both and declared the soul to be a self-moving number

src.q: [defines it as] a number moving itself

s: Kaṭha I.3.3 (Hume 1921) pictures the ātman as the lord riding in the chariot of the body, with buddhi as driver, manas as reins and the senses as horses; Hume heads it 'Parable of the individual soul in a chariot'. s: Evans-Wentz's Tibetan Book of the Dead (1927) renders the consciousness that leaves the body at death as the 'consciousness-principle', which at first 'hath fainted away', and his commentary says the Bardo body, an exact duplicate of the human body in an 'ethereal-like' matter, retains that principle.

src.l: W. Y. Evans-Wentz (ed.), Kazi Dawa-Samdup (trans.), 1927, The Tibetan Book of the Dead (Bardo Thodol)
src.q: The common people call this the state wherein the consciousness-principle hath fainted away.

s: The Tibetan Zhi khro dgongs pa rang grol (Karma Lingpa's cycle, 14th c.) addresses the dead: the consciousness-mind (rnam shes sems) has shown its impermanence and, by the power of karma, taken another body; another verse calls 'the consciousness of the bardo in a bodiless form of light'.

s: 'Soul' in SL's 19th–20th-century Indian translations stands for at least five different words: ātman (Hume), puruṣa (Davies), jīva (the usual rendering Ghoshal refused), dehin (Schlegel's spiritus, Arnold's spirit) and the Milindapañha's vedagū and puggala (Rhys Davids). So 'Buddhism denies the soul' is ambiguous: the Buddhist texts deny an attā/puggala as a real referent, not the Jain jīva or the Sāṃkhya puruṣa, and they keep a transmigrating viññāṇa/rnam shes.

src.l: Robert Ernest Hume (trans.), 1921, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads
src.q: That is Ātman (Soul).

src.l: Ishvarakrishna, John Davies (trans.), 1881, Hindu Philosophy: The Sankhya Karika of Iswara Krishna
src.q: it is proved that there is a plurality of souls.

src.l: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), 1879, The Questions of King Milinda, Part 1 (SBE Vol. 35)
src.q: there is no permanent individuality (no soul) implied in his name

s: The chariot is often offered as a shared Indo-Greek image of the soul, but on SL's pages it serves three incompatible doctrines: in the Phaedrus the soul is the whole team, in the Kaṭha the self is a passenger who is neither driver (buddhi) nor reins (manas), and in the Milindapañha the chariot is a name for parts with no owner, used to deny the self.

src.l: Robert Ernest Hume (trans.), 1921, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads
src.q: Know thou the soul (ātman, self) as riding in a chariot

src.l: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), 1879, The Questions of King Milinda, Part 1 (SBE Vol. 35)
src.q: Chariot is a mere empty sound.

s: Avicenna (Shifāʾ, Kitāb al-Nafs I.1, c. 1020–27), in the Arabic: a man created at once, sight veiled, falling in air or void with limbs apart, would not doubt the existence of his self (dhāt) yet would affirm none of his limbs, organs, 'nor heart, nor blood'; so the self affirmed is other than what is not affirmed.

src.l: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), 1027, al-Shifa (The Cure): Philosophy and Medicine
src.q: He would not doubt affirming his self as existing, yet he would not affirm with it any of his limbs, nor any of his internal organs, nor heart, nor blood, nor anything external.
src.qo: فلا يشك في اثباته لذاته موجودا ولا يثبت مع ذلك طرفا من اعضائه ولا باطنا من احشائه ولا قلبا ولا دما

s: In the c. 1500 Latin print of Avicenna's De anima I.1 (scan 7) the floating man affirms neither 'animum' nor 'cerebrum', and SL's English follows it ('nor the soul, nor the brain'), where the Arabic of the Shifāʾ has 'nor heart, nor blood' (lā qalban wa-lā daman): the Latin as printed makes the self-affirming man deny he affirms a soul.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.q: He will not doubt, indeed, to affirm himself to be, but he will not affirm the exteriors of his members, nor the hidden things of his interiors, nor the soul, nor the brain, nor anything of such things.
src.qo: nec oculta ſuoz interiorz nec animuz.nec cere brum

s: Avicenna's De anima V.2 (Latin, c. 1500 print) argues that the substance in man that receives intelligibles is not a body, nor has its being through the body as a faculty or form in it: the rational soul is 'not imprinted in bodily matter'.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.loc: De anima V.2, chapter heading and opening; scan 80
src.q: There is no doubt about this, that in man there is some substance that apprehends intelligibles by receiving. We will say, therefore, that the substance that is in the subject of intelligibles is not a body, nor has it being on account of the body in any way, as its faculty or its form.
src.qo: Capitulum de affirmanda existentia anime rationalis non impressa in materia corporali.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.q: Capitulum de affirmanda existentia anime rationalis non impressa in materia corporali.

s: Avicenna's De anima V.3 (Latin) holds that individual souls are not eternal but begin to exist with a body, which is created as the soul's 'kingdom and instrument', and that each soul has a natural inclination to rule that one body: no pre-existence.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.q: The singularity, therefore, of souls is something that begins to exist and is not eternal, which would have been always. It begins to exist with the body only.
src.qo: Singularitas ergo anima rum est aliquid quod esse incipit et non est eternum quod fuerit semper.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.q: Singularitas ergo anima rum est aliquid quod esse incipit et non est eternum quod fuerit semper.

s: Avicenna's Shifāʾ, Kitāb al-Nafs V.4 (c. 1020–27), heads a chapter 'that the human soul does not perish and does not transmigrate' and argues that the soul does not die with the body's death, since what perishes with another depends on it, and the soul's tie to the body is not of that kind.

src.l: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), 1027, al-Shifa (The Cure): Philosophy and Medicine
src.q: Chapter Four: On the human soul not perishing nor transmigrating As for the soul not dying with the death of the body: this is because everything that perishes due to the perishing of another thing is attached to it by some kind of attachment.
src.qo: الفصل الرابع في ان النفس الانسانية لا تفسد ولا تناسخ اما ان النفس لا تموت بموت البدن

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.q: which is the power ordered in the middle cavity of the brain where the worm is, and it is accustomed to compose something of that which is in the imagination with another

s: Avicenna's De anima I (Latin) promises to show that 'the soul is one', its powers flowing from it into the limbs, and that the soul in every animal gathers and composes the matter of its body and preserves it.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin

s: The Latin Compendium de anima ascribed to Avicenna (Alpago, Venice 1546) says that after death the rational soul, separated from the body, keeps the perfection it gained through the senses, and understands more easily than in life, no longer hindered by bodily passions.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), Andrea Alpago (trans.), 1546, Compendium de anima
src.q: Therefore, after death, the rational soul is separated from the body with the extraction of those animal and vegetative powers—that is, with the perfection acquired from those very powers.

s: Al-Kindī's treatise on the intellect (9th c., medieval Latin De intellectu, Nagy 1897) says an apprehended form is in the soul not as a thing in a vessel nor as a carving in a body, 'for the soul is not a body nor is it circumscribed'; the soul is one thing, and the sensing power is the soul itself.

src.l: al-Kindī, 1897, Die philosophischen Abhandlungen des al-Kindi
src.q: However, it is not in the soul like something in a vessel, nor like a carving in a body; for the soul is not a body nor is it circumscribed.
src.qo: non est autem in anima sicut aliquid in uase, nec sicut caelatura in corpore; quoniam anima non est corpus nec circumscripta.

s: Al-Fārābī's Virtuous City (c. 942–50; Dieterici's German, 1900) holds that the souls of the ignorant cities remain incomplete and need matter to exist, so with their matter they 'perish and turn to nothing' like beasts and snakes, while the citizens of the virtuous city have souls freed from matter.

s: Al-Ghazālī's Tahāfut al-falāsifa (1095) devotes its 18th to 20th discussions to the soul: against the philosophers' claim that the human soul is a self-subsistent substance neither body nor accident, that annihilation is impossible for it, and their denial of bodily resurrection.

src.l: al-Ghazālī, n.d., Tahafut al-Falasifa (Incoherence of the Philosophers)
src.loc: Introduction, list of the twenty discussions; scan 51
src.q: soul is a self-subsistent substance that is neither body nor accident. The nineteenth: On [refuting] their assertion that annihilation is impossible for the human soul. The twentieth: On refuting their denial of bodily resurrection

s: In the Tahāfut's discussion of the world's eternity, al-Ghazālī reports a view that the soul depends on the composition of the body, so that death is its annihilation and souls exist only among the living.

src.l: al-Ghazālī, n.d., Tahafut al-Falasifa (Incoherence of the Philosophers)
src.loc: Discussion 1 (running head 'Discussion 4' as OCR'd), printed p. 83; scan 195
src.q: Others have said that the soul is dependent on the composition of the body and that the meaning of death is its annihilation, [as] it has no subsistence in terms of its [own] substance without the body.

s: Al-Ghazālī's Kīmiyā-yi saʿādat (c. 1105; Homes's English, 1873) says the spirit 'which we call heart' has no size, divisibility, form or colour, and that the soul 'exists by the will of God: it has neither quantity or physical quality; it is exempt from being known'.

src.l: Al-Ghazali, Henry A. Homes (trans.), 1873, The Alchemy of Happiness
src.loc: ch. on knowledge of God; scan 57
src.q: The spirit, for example, which we call heart is exempt from the entrance of fancies and imaginations, and also from size and divisibility.

src.l: Al-Ghazali, Henry A. Homes (trans.), 1873, The Alchemy of Happiness
src.q: It exists by the will of God: it has neither quantity or physical quality; it is exempt from being known.

s: Al-Ghazālī's Mishkāt al-anwār (c. 1106–11; Gairdner's English, 1924) reads the Light Verse (Qur'an 24:35) as five human spirits: the sensory spirit is the niche, the imaginative the glass, and so on up to 'the transcendental prophetic spirit' of saints and prophets, the oil that is 'well-nigh luminant, though Fire touched it not.'

src.l: al-Ghazālī, W. H. T. Gairdner (trans.), 1924, Mishkat al-Anwar (The Niche for Lights)
src.q: 1. Consider the sensory spirit. Its lights, you observe, come through several apertures, the eyes, ears, nostrils, etc. Now the aptest symbol for this, in our world of experience, is the Niche for a lamp in a wall.

src.l: al-Ghazālī, W. H. T. Gairdner (trans.), 1924, Mishkat al-Anwar (The Niche for Lights)
src.q: 5. The transcendental prophetic spirit, which is possessed by saints as well as prophets if it is absolutely luminous and clear.

s: Qur'an 17:85 answers the question about the rūḥ: 'the spirit is from the command (amr) of my Lord', and little knowledge of it is given; Palmer (1880) prints 'The spirit comes at the bidding of my Lord', and SL's English of al-Hujwīrī's Persian quotation renders it 'the spirit is of the command of my Lord'.

src.loc: Sura XVII.87 in Palmer's numbering (17:85); scan 24
src.q: They will ask thee of the spirit¹. Say, 'The spirit comes at the bidding of my Lord, and ye are given but a little knowledge thereof.'

s: Al-Hujwīrī's Kashf al-Maḥjūb (c. 1060–72) uses Qur'an 17:85 against 'heretics' who call the spirit (rūḥ) eternal, worship it, call it the 'Divine Spirit' and make it pass from person to person; he says this error is shared by the Christians and by India, Tibet and China.

s: Al-Hujwīrī (Kashf al-Maḥjūb) reports that nafs is taken by some to mean the spirit, by others manliness, the body or blood, but that the Sufi masters agree its reality is 'the source of evil and the basis of wickedness', whether an essence lodged in the frame like the spirit or an attribute of it like life; SL's English renders nafs 'self'.

src.l: ʿAlī al-Hujwīrī, V. A. Zhukovsky (ed.), 1926, Kashf al-Maḥjūb (Persian critical edition)
src.loc: chapter on mortification of the nafs; scan 256 (SL English)
src.q: But to the realized masters of this group, the intention behind this word is none of these. They agree that the reality of it is the source of evil and the basis of wickedness.

s: A Persian treatise copied in a Fez compilation of 1576 lists the levels of the nafs as ammāra (commanding), lawwāma (reproaching), mulhima (inspired), muṭmaʾinna (at peace), rāḍiya (content) and marḍiyya (well-pleasing), and says the rational soul is in itself a substance detached from matter, called 'soul' when it governs a body as a king his kingdom.

src.l: Anonymous (Persian treatise in a Fez compilation), 1576, Compilation of texts on logic and astronomy (Fez, 1576)
src.loc: Persian treatise on the levels of the nafs; scan 111 (Persian)

src.l: Anonymous (Persian treatise in a Fez compilation), 1576, Compilation of texts on logic and astronomy (Fez, 1576)
src.q: is, in its essence, a substance detached from matter and material attachments.
