s: Macdonald (1909) reports al-Ghazālī's two usages of nafs: the 'soul that commands to evil' (Qur'an 12:53), comprising anger and lust and altogether blameworthy, and the praiseworthy nafs that is 'the very essence of man which knows God'.

src.l: Duncan Black Macdonald, 1909, The Religious Attitude and Life in Islam
src.loc: Lecture on the discipline of the traveller, printed p. 230; scan 254
src.q: it is altogether blameworthy, while the soul of the second usage is praiseworthy as the very essence of man which knows God and all knowable things.

s: Ibn Ṭufayl's Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān (c. 1160–85) says 'heart' (qalb) is said of three things: the body of the heart, the spirit (rūḥ) in its cavity, and the form of that spirit, overflowing with its powers upon the human body; what Ḥayy saw enters none of the three.

src.l: Ibn Ṭufayl, Edward Pococke (Latin trans.), 1671, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān / Philosophus Autodidactus, sive Epistola Abi Jaafar Ebn Tophail de Hai Ebn Yokdhan
src.q: I do not mean by the "heart" the physical heart, nor the spirit in its cavity, but I mean the form of that spirit overflowing with its powers upon the human body.
src.qo: ولست اعني بالقلب جسم القلب ولا الروح الذي في تجويفه بل اعني به صورة تلك الروح الفايضة بقواها علي بدن الانسان

src.l: Ibn Ṭufayl, Edward Pococke (Latin trans.), 1671, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān / Philosophus Autodidactus, sive Epistola Abi Jaafar Ebn Tophail de Hai Ebn Yokdhan
src.q: ولست اعني بالقلب جسم القلب ولا الروح الذي في تجويفه بل اعني به صورة تلك الروح الفايضة بقواها علي بدن الانسان

s: In Ibn Ṭufayl's Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, Ḥayy reasons that the Necessary Being can be perceived only by something that is neither body nor a faculty in a body, and since he has perceived Him, the essence (dhāt) by which he perceives is non-corporeal.

src.l: Ibn Ṭufayl, Edward Pococke (Latin trans.), 1671, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān / Philosophus Autodidactus, sive Epistola Abi Jaafar Ebn Tophail de Hai Ebn Yokdhan
src.q: Therefore, it became clear to him by this that the essence by which he perceived Him is something non-corporeal, and it is not permissible that any of the attributes of bodies should apply to it.
src.qo: فتبين له بذلك ان ذاته التي ادركه بها امر غير جسماني ولا يجوز عليه شيء من صفات الاجسام

s: Averroes (al-Kashf ʿan manāhij al-adilla, c. 1179, Arabic, Cairo 1910) builds the view he calls fittest for the elite on two points: that the soul endures (al-nafs bāqiya), and that its return to other bodies avoids the absurdities of the return of the very same bodies, whose matter passes from person to person.

src.l: Averroes (Ibn Rushd), 1910, Kitāb Falsafat Ibn Rushd (Philosophy of Averroes), Arabic
src.loc: section on the Return (maʿād); scan 136 (SL English)
src.q: Second, that the return of the soul to other bodies does not result in the same logical impossibilities that arise from the return of those exact same bodies.
src.qo: أحدها أن النفس باقية . والثاني انه ليس يلحق عن عودة النفس الى أجسام أخر المحال الذي يلحق عن عودة تلك الاجسام بعينها

src.l: Averroes (Ibn Rushd), 1910, Kitāb Falsafat Ibn Rushd (Philosophy of Averroes), Arabic
src.q: أحدها أن النفس باقية . والثاني انه ليس يلحق عن عودة النفس الى أجسام أخر المحال الذي يلحق عن عودة تلك الاجسام بعينها

s: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (10th c.; Dieterici's German, 1868) argue that the soul is a substance, not an accident, from motion: a natural cause drives a body one way, but animal motion goes many ways by will and choice, and so is called 'of the soul' (seelisch).

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, Friedrich Dieterici (trans.), 1868, Die Logik und Psychologie der Araber im zehnten Jahrhundert n. Chr.
src.q: Es bleibt noch übrig zu zeigen, dass die Seele eine Substanz und kein Accidens sei

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, Friedrich Dieterici (trans.), 1868, Die Logik und Psychologie der Araber im zehnten Jahrhundert n. Chr.
src.q: From these three premises, the existence of the soul emerges.
src.qo: Es bleibt noch übrig zu zeigen, dass die Seele eine Substanz und kein Accidens sei

s: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Dieterici's German) define man as a whole made of a mortal body and a living (immortal) soul: life is nothing but the soul's using the body for its work, death its ceasing to do so, waking its use of the five senses and sleep the pause of that use.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, Friedrich Dieterici (trans.), 1868, Die Logik und Psychologie der Araber im zehnten Jahrhundert n. Chr.
src.q: Leben besteht nur darin, dass die Seele den Körper zu ihrem Werk verwendet, und Tod ist nichts andres als dass die Seele diese Anwendung unterlässt.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, Friedrich Dieterici (trans.), 1868, Die Logik und Psychologie der Araber im zehnten Jahrhundert n. Chr.
src.q: Life consists only in the soul using the body for its work, and death is nothing other than the soul ceasing this application.
src.qo: Leben besteht nur darin, dass die Seele den Körper zu ihrem Werk verwendet, und Tod ist nichts andres als dass die Seele diese Anwendung unterlässt.

s: Critique: al-Ghazālī's Tahāfut (Discussions 18–20, as Marmura's introduction summarises them) holds that Avicenna's proofs that the soul is immaterial are not demonstrative, and that even granting an immaterial soul, bodily resurrection remains possible, so the philosophers' denial of it fails.

src.l: al-Ghazālī, n.d., Tahafut al-Falasifa (Incoherence of the Philosophers)
src.q: Al-Ghazālī argues in detail that the theory of the soul’s immateriality, on which Avicenna’s denial is based, has not been demonstrated.

s: Critique: Avicenna himself raises against the floating man the objection that what is self-perceived is the temperament (mizāj), the body's blend, and answers only that the temperament is perceived through being affected; the reply asserts rather than shows that self-awareness is not the awareness of a bodily state, which is the gap a functionalist (or machine) reading of the self would exploit.

src.l: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), 1027, al-Shifa (The Cure): Philosophy and Medicine
src.q: If it is said that what is perceived is the temperament, the answer is that the temperament is only perceived through affection
src.qo: ان المشعور به هو المزاج

src.l: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), 1027, al-Shifa (The Cure): Philosophy and Medicine
src.q: ان المشعور به هو المزاج

s: Kant (Kritik der reinen Vernunft, A 1781, critique of the second paralogism, A360-61) allows anyone to claim that 'the thinking I, the soul' (a name for the transcendental object of inner sense) is simple, but says the expression applies to no actual object, so rational psychology falls with its main support.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.loc: A360-61, critique of the 2nd paralogism (SL English); scan 341
src.q: This expression nevertheless has no application that extends to actual objects and therefore cannot expand our knowledge in the slightest.
src.qo: das denkende Ich, die Seele, (ein Name für den transscendentalen Gegenstand des inneren Sinnes) sei einfach; dieser Ausdruck hat deshalb doch gar keinen auf wirkliche Gegenstände sich erstreckenden Gebrauch

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: das denkende Ich, die Seele, (ein Name für den transscendentalen Gegenstand des inneren Sinnes) sei einfach; dieser Ausdruck hat deshalb doch gar keinen auf wirkliche Gegenstände sich erstreckenden Gebrauch

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: Thus, the whole of rational psychology collapses along with its main support.
src.qo: das denkende Ich, die Seele, (ein Name für den transscendentalen Gegenstand des inneren Sinnes) sei einfach; dieser Ausdruck hat deshalb doch gar keinen auf wirkliche Gegenstände sich erstreckenden Gebrauch

s: Kant (KrV A361-63, 1781) states the third paralogism (what is conscious of the numerical identity of itself at different times is a person; the soul is; so it is a person) and answers that the identity of consciousness across time is only a formal condition of my thoughts and does not prove the numerical identity of my subject.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: Whatever is conscious of the numerical identity of its self at different times is, to that extent, a person. Now, the soul, etc. Therefore, it is a person.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: The identity of the consciousness of myself in different times is therefore only a formal condition of my thoughts and their connection, but it does not at all prove the numerical identity of my subject
src.qo: Es ist also die Identität des Bewusstseins Meiner selbst in verschiedenen Zeiten nur eine formale Bedingung meiner Gedanken und ihres Zusammenhanges, beweiset aber gar nicht die numerische Identität, meines Subjects

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: Es ist also die Identität des Bewusstseins Meiner selbst in verschiedenen Zeiten nur eine formale Bedingung meiner Gedanken und ihres Zusammenhanges, beweiset aber gar nicht die numerische Identität, meines Subjects

s: Kant (KrV A402-3, 1781) names the error of 'rational psychology' (rationale Seelenlehre) a sophisma figurae dictionis: the major premise uses the category of substance only transcendentally, the minor applies it empirically to the soul without first establishing its persistence; the illusion is 'the subreption of hypostatised consciousness'.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: Man könnte ihn die Subreption des hypostasirten Bewusstseins (apperceptionis substantiatae) nennen.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: In the minor premise, however, the very same concept is applied to the object of all inner experience, without, however, pre-establishing and basing it on the condition of its application
src.qo: Man könnte ihn die Subreption des hypostasirten Bewusstseins (apperceptionis substantiatae) nennen. … Wenn man den Paralogism in den dialektischen Vernunftschlüssen der rationalen Seelenlehre, sofern sie gleichwol richtige Prämissen haben, logisch betiteln will

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: Wenn man den Paralogism in den dialektischen Vernunftschlüssen der rationalen Seelenlehre, sofern sie gleichwol richtige Prämissen haben, logisch betiteln will

s: Kant's refutation of Mendelssohn (KrV B413-14, 1787): even granting the soul is simple, with no extensive magnitude, it has intensive magnitude, a degree of reality in all its powers, which can sink through infinitely many smaller degrees, so it could cease by gradual remission (remissio) without division; simplicity proves no persistence.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: Widerlegung des Mendelssohnschen Beweises der Beharrlichkeit der Seele.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: though not through division, could indeed cease to exist through the gradual slackening (<term>remissio</term> <gloss>remission/diminution</gloss>) of its powers.
src.qo: Widerlegung des Mendelssohnschen Beweises der Beharrlichkeit der Seele. … obgleich nicht durch Zertheilung, doch durch allmähliche Nachlassung (remissio) ihrer Kräfte

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1878, Kritik der reinen Vernunft
src.q: obgleich nicht durch Zertheilung, doch durch allmähliche Nachlassung (remissio) ihrer Kräfte

s: Mendelssohn's Phaedon (1767; SL has the 1768 edition), first dialogue: Socrates argues there is no middle between being and non-being, so passing from one to the other would be a sudden change without transition, which nature cannot produce; nature can therefore bring about neither existence nor annihilation.

src.l: Moses Mendelssohn, 1768, Phaedon oder über die Unsterblichkeit der Seele
src.loc: First dialogue, printed p. 104 (SL English); scan 122
src.q: Being and non-being would thus be two states that follow immediately upon one another, which would have to be the closest to each other: but we have seen that nature can produce no such changes that must happen suddenly and without transition.
src.qo: Seyn und Nichtseyn wären also zween Zustände, die unmittelbar aufeinander folgen, die sich einander die nächsten seyn müßten

src.l: Moses Mendelssohn, 1768, Phaedon oder über die Unsterblichkeit der Seele
src.q: Seyn und Nichtseyn wären also zween Zustände, die unmittelbar aufeinander folgen, die sich einander die nächsten seyn müßten

s: In the third dialogue of Mendelssohn's Phaedon (1767), once Cebes grants that the soul is a simple being with its own subsistence and is imperishable, the remaining doubt is whether God will keep the human Geist awake and conscious after death or let it sink into a sleep-like state; Socrates turns from the nature of things to the divine perfections to settle it.

src.l: Moses Mendelssohn, 1768, Phaedon oder über die Unsterblichkeit der Seele
src.loc: Third dialogue, printed p. 166 (SL English); scan 184
src.q: You grant, my friend! that the soul is a simple being that has its own subsistence without the body: do you not? — Correct! — You further admit that it is imperishable?

src.l: Moses Mendelssohn, 1768, Phaedon oder über die Unsterblichkeit der Seele
src.q: Will he let the spirit of man continue in eternity in a waking state, well aware of the present and the past?
src.qo: Wird er den Geist des Menschen in einem wachenden Zustande, des Gegenwärtigen und des Vergangenen wohl bewußt, in Ewigkeit fortdauern lassen?

src.l: Moses Mendelssohn, 1768, Phaedon oder über die Unsterblichkeit der Seele
src.q: Wird er den Geist des Menschen in einem wachenden Zustande, des Gegenwärtigen und des Vergangenen wohl bewußt, in Ewigkeit fortdauern lassen?

s: Wolff (Psychologia rationalis §731, 1734) argues that because the soul is a simple substance (§48) it cannot perish in the way composite things do, the body being composite; he adds that this agrees with Christ's teaching that the soul cannot be killed as the body is.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1734, Psychologia rationalis
src.q: Anima eodem modo, quo corpus interit, interire nequit. Anima enim substantia simplex est (§. 48)

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1734, Psychologia rationalis
src.q: The soul cannot perish in the same way that the body perishes. For the soul is a "simple substance"
src.qo: Anima eodem modo, quo corpus interit, interire nequit. Anima enim substantia simplex est (§. 48)

s: Wolff (Psychologia empirica §1, 1732) defines empirical psychology as the science of establishing the principles of psychology through experience, giving the reason of what happens in the human soul, and keeps it apart from rational psychology, whose principles are still disputed; the dedication of his Psychologia rationalis (1734) calls the latter a sublime philosophy leading to the inner knowledge of the soul.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1732, Psychologia empirica
src.q: Psychologia empirica est scientia stabiliendi Psychologiæ principia per experientiam, unde ratio redditur eorum, quæ in anima humana fiunt.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1732, Psychologia empirica
src.q: Empirical psychology is the science of establishing the principles of psychology through experience, whence an account is given of those things which occur in the human soul.
src.qo: Psychologia empirica est scientia stabiliendi Psychologiæ principia per experientiam, unde ratio redditur eorum, quæ in anima humana fiunt.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1734, Psychologia rationalis
src.q: Sublimem philosophiam continet Pſychologia rationalis, quæ ad interiorem animæ noſtræ cognitionem manuducit.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1734, Psychologia rationalis
src.q: nourishing the soul with a pleasure that cannot be found elsewhere
src.qo: Sublimem philosophiam continet Pſychologia rationalis, quæ ad interiorem animæ noſtræ cognitionem manuducit.

s: Havenreuter's thesis print (SL record 1591) is titled ΨΥΧΟΛΟΓΙΑ sive philosophica de animo, a disputation excerpted from Aristotle's three books de Animo: the Greek coinage psychologia names Aristotle's De anima matter, and the Latin title renders psychē as animus, not anima.

src.l: Johann Ludwig Havenreuter, 1591, Psychologia: sive philosophica, de animo syzetesis, ex libris tribus Aristotelis peri psyches
src.q: ΨΥΧΟΛΟΓΙΑ sive PHILOSOPHICA DE ANIMO συζήτησις ex tribus de Animo Aristotelis libris excerpta.

src.l: Johann Ludwig Havenreuter, 1591, Psychologia: sive philosophica, de animo syzetesis, ex libris tribus Aristotelis peri psyches
src.q: quam Animum esse aliquid: licet quid sit incognitum pene incertum atque inexploratum habeamus.

s: Fechner (Elemente der Psychophysik I, ch. II, 1860) defines psychophysics as an exact theory of the functional or dependency relations between body and soul (Körper und Seele), counting as the soul's domain whatever inner perception grasps, and restricts it to the side of appearance without going back to the essence of body or soul.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1860, Elemente der Psychophysik, Erster Theil
src.q: Unter Psychophysik soll hier eine exacte Lehre von den functionellen oder Abhängigkeitsbeziehungen zwischen Körper und Seele, allgemeiner zwischen körperlicher und geistiger, physischer und psychischer, Welt verstanden werden.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1860, Elemente der Psychophysik, Erster Theil
src.q: By psychophysics, we should here understand an exact theory of the functional or dependency relationships between the body and the soul
src.qo: Unter Psychophysik soll hier eine exacte Lehre von den functionellen oder Abhängigkeitsbeziehungen zwischen Körper und Seele, allgemeiner zwischen körperlicher und geistiger, physischer und psychischer, Welt verstanden werden.

s: SL's English of Fechner's Elemente der Psychophysik (1860) renders Körper und Geist as 'body and mind' (scan 21) but Körper und Seele as 'body and soul' (scan 22), and Erfahrungsseelenlehre ('experiential soul-doctrine') as 'empirical psychology'.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1860, Elemente der Psychophysik, Erster Theil
src.q: gleichgültig für die Auffassungsweise der Grundbeziehung von Körper und Geist

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1860, Elemente der Psychophysik, Erster Theil
src.q: indifferent to the way we perceive the fundamental relationship between body and mind
src.qo: gleichgültig für die Auffassungsweise der Grundbeziehung von Körper und Geist

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1860, Elemente der Psychophysik, Erster Theil
src.q: and with the psychological in the sense of empirical psychology
src.qo: auf das Psychische im Sinne der Erfahrungsseelenlehre

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1860, Elemente der Psychophysik, Erster Theil
src.q: auf das Psychische im Sinne der Erfahrungsseelenlehre

s: Fechner (Nanna, 1848) asks why we never say an artificial flower smiles at us as a living one does, however alike they are, and answers that we sense a truly laughing soul only in the living one; he calls those who see the signs of a living soul in plants and still refuse to believe worse than the Jews who demanded signs.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: Und warum sagen wir nie eben so von einer künſtlichen Blume, daß sie uns anläche wie eine lebendige, sei sie auch noch so ähnlich der lebendigen? Warum anders, als weil wir nur in dieser nicht in jener eine wirklich lachende Seele ahnen.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: And why do we never say of an artificial flower that it smiles at us like a living one, however similar it might be to the living?
src.qo: Und warum sagen wir nie eben so von einer künſtlichen Blume, daß sie uns anläche wie eine lebendige, sei sie auch noch so ähnlich der lebendigen? Warum anders, als weil wir nur in dieser nicht in jener eine wirklich lachende Seele ahnen.

s: Carus (Psyche, 1846) speaks of 'in themselves unconscious processes' in which we must presuppose the bodily condition of a mental stirring, more delicate than anything weighable or measurable, and argues that a disease that permanently retunes parts of the nerve substance must permanently retune the mental stirrings too.

src.l: Carl Gustav Carus, 1846, Psyche: zur Entwicklungsgeschichte der Seele
src.q: Noch viel zarter jedoch, und für Alles, was wir wägbar und meßbar nennen, gänzlich unerreichbar, hat man jene an und für sich unbewußten Vorgänge zu betrachten, in denen wir die leibliche Bedingung einer geistigen Regung voraussetzen müssen!

s: Brentano (Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte I.1, 1874) reports the view that neither sensation nor inner perception shows a substance, so psychology is the science of psychic phenomena, not of the soul: 'a soul does not exist, at least not for us', and quotes Albert Lange's paradox of 'a psychology without a soul' (Geschichte des Materialismus, 1st ed. 1866, p. 465).

src.l: Franz Brentano, 1874, Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte, Bd. 1
src.loc: Bk I ch. 1, printed p. 13 (German); scan 32
src.q: Ein Seele gibt es nicht, wenigstens nicht für uns; eine Psychologie kann und soll es nichtsdestoweniger geben; aber — um den paradoxen Ausdruck von Albert Lange zu gebrauchen — eine Psychologie ohne Seele

src.l: Franz Brentano, 1874, Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte, Bd. 1
src.q: Also nur ruhig eine Psychologie ohne Seele angenommen!

src.l: Franz Brentano, 1874, Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte, Bd. 1
src.q: A soul does not exist, at least not for us; a psychology can and should nonetheless exist; but—to use the paradoxical expression of Albert Lange—a psychology without a soul.
src.qo: Ein Seele gibt es nicht, wenigstens nicht für uns; eine Psychologie kann und soll es nichtsdestoweniger geben; aber — um den paradoxen Ausdruck von Albert Lange zu gebrauchen — eine Psychologie ohne Seele … Also nur ruhig eine Psychologie ohne Seele angenommen!

s: William James (Principles of Psychology I, ch. X 'The Consciousness of Self', 1890) says that calling the 'more' behind thought and brain-state a Soul explains nothing; metaphysically he finds an anima mundi thinking in all of us more promising than many individual souls, but as psychologists 'the passing Thought itself is the only verifiable thinker'.

src.l: William James, 1890, The Principles of Psychology, Vol. I
src.q: Meanwhile, as psychologists, we need not be metaphysical at all. The phenomena are enough, the passing Thought itself is the only verifiable thinker, and its empirical connection with the brain-process is the ultimate known law.

src.l: William James, 1890, The Principles of Psychology, Vol. I
src.q: I find the notion of some sort of an anima mundi thinking in all of us to be a more promising hypothesis, in spite of all its difficulties, than that of a lot of absolutely individual souls.

s: James (Principles I, ch. X, 1890) says the 'Spiritualists' (the soul-substance philosophers) deduce no property of mental life from known properties of the soul, but find characters ready-made in mental life and 'clap them into the Soul'; the Soul is 'an outbirth' of the maxim he credits to Hodgson: 'Whatever you are totally ignorant of, assert to be the explanation of everything else.'

src.l: William James, 1890, The Principles of Psychology, Vol. I
src.q: They simply find various characters ready-made in the mental life, and these they clap into the Soul, saying, "Lo! behold the source from whence they flow!"

src.l: William James, 1890, The Principles of Psychology, Vol. I
src.q: Altogether, the Soul is an outbirth of that sort of philosophizing whose great maxim, according to Dr. Hodgson, is: "Whatever you are totally ignorant of, assert to be the explanation of everything else."

s: James (Principles I, ch. IX 'The Stream of Thought', 1890) says consciousness does not appear to itself chopped up in bits; it is nothing jointed but flows, and he names it 'the stream of thought, of consciousness, or of subjective life'.

src.l: William James, 1890, The Principles of Psychology, Vol. I
src.q: It is nothing jointed; it flows. A 'river' or a 'stream' are the metaphors by which it is most naturally described. In talking of it hereafter, let us call it the stream of thought, of consciousness, or of subjective life.

s: Kardec's Livre des Esprits (1857; SL has an 1860 edition), Introduction, summarises the spirits' teaching: the qualities of the soul are those of the Spirit incarnated in us; the soul had its individuality before incarnation and keeps it after; the Spirit passes through several, always progressive incarnations, and 'the soul or Spirit' is never incarnated in an animal.

src.l: Allan Kardec, 1857, Le Livre des Esprits
src.loc: Introduction, printed p. XVI (SL English); scan 26
src.q: The qualities of the soul are those of the Spirit incarnated within us; thus, a good man is the incarnation of a good Spirit, and a perverse man that of an impure Spirit.
src.qo: Les qualités de l’âme sont celles de l’Esprit qui est incarné

src.l: Allan Kardec, 1857, Le Livre des Esprits
src.q: Les qualités de l’âme sont celles de l’Esprit qui est incarné

src.l: Allan Kardec, 1857, Le Livre des Esprits
src.q: The soul possessed its individuality before its incarnation; it retains it after its separation from the body.
src.qo: Les qualités de l’âme sont celles de l’Esprit qui est incarné

s: Kardec (Livre des Esprits II.1, qq. 93-94, 1857) calls the vaporous substance enveloping the Spirit, by analogy with a seed's perisperm, the 'périsprit'; the spirits answer that this semi-material envelope is drawn from the universal fluid of each globe, so the Spirit changes it, like clothing, when it passes from one world to another.

src.l: Allan Kardec, 1857, Le Livre des Esprits
src.q: Comme le germe d’un fruit est entouré du périsperme, de même l’Esprit proprement dit est environné d’une enveloppe que, par comparaison, on peut appeler périsprit.

src.l: Allan Kardec, 1857, Le Livre des Esprits
src.q: In moving from one world to another, the Spirit changes its envelope, just as you change your clothes.
src.qo: Comme le germe d’un fruit est entouré du périsperme, de même l’Esprit proprement dit est environné d’une enveloppe que, par comparaison, on peut appeler périsprit.

s: Blavatsky (The Key to Theosophy, 1889) tabulates the 'Theosophical division' of man under Sanskrit terms: a lower quaternary of Rupa or Sthula-Sarira (physical body), Prana (life), Linga Sharira (astral body, the double) and Kama rupa (seat of animal desires), and an upper triad of Manas (mind), Buddhi (the Spiritual Soul) and Atma (Spirit, one with the Absolute).

src.l: Helena Blavatsky, 1889, The Key to Theosophy
src.loc: sect. VI, printed p. 91, Lower Quaternary; scan 109
src.q:
(c) Linga Sharira.  (c) Astral body.  (c) The Double, the phantom body.
(d) Kama rupa.  (d) The seat of animal desires and passions.

src.l: Helena Blavatsky, 1889, The Key to Theosophy
src.loc: printed p. 92, Upper Imperishable Triad; scan 110
src.q:
(f) Buddhi.  (f) The Spiritual Soul.  (f) The vehicle of pure universal spirit.
(g) Atma.  (g) Spirit.  (g) One with the Absolute, as its radiation.

s: Blavatsky (Key to Theosophy IX, 1889) says that at death the lower three principles (body, life, astral double) leave the man for ever, while kama-rupa, the animal soul, and the higher triad find themselves in Kama-loka, an astral locality she equates with the limbus of scholastic theology and the Hades of the ancients, where the astral eidolons of all beings, animals included, await their second death.

src.l: Helena Blavatsky, 1889, The Key to Theosophy
src.loc: ch. IX 'On the Kama-loka and Devachan'; scan 161
src.q: The latter is an astral locality, the limbus of scholastic theology, the Hades of the ancients, and, strictly speaking, a locality only in a relative sense.

src.l: Helena Blavatsky, 1889, The Key to Theosophy
src.q: it is there that the astral <term>eidolons</term> of all the beings that have lived, animals included, await their second death.

s: Leadbeater (The Astral Plane, 1895) says that between earth-life and the heaven-world man casts off and leaves to slow disintegration 'no less than three corpses', the dense physical body, the etheric double and the astral vehicle, whose matter is reused on their respective planes; the abandoned astral shell is devoid of consciousness and intelligence.

src.l: Charles Webster Leadbeater, 1895, The Astral Plane: Its Scenery, Inhabitants and Phenomena
src.loc: Inhabitants, Human: dead; printed p. 54; scan 58
src.q: man casts off and leaves to slow disintegration no less than three corpses—the dense physical body, the etheric double, and the astral vehicle—all of which are by degrees resolved into their constituent elements

src.l: Charles Webster Leadbeater, 1895, The Astral Plane: Its Scenery, Inhabitants and Phenomena
src.q: This also, like the other kind of shell, is entirely devoid of consciousness and intelligence

s: Against reading the seven principles as an Indian doctrine: on the same pages Blavatsky presses Plato's nous and psuche, Paul's psychical and spiritual body, and the Egyptians into the septenary, and concedes in a footnote that numbering the principles is 'strictly speaking, useless' and that Sinnett had called three of them the Animal, Human and Spiritual Souls; the Sanskrit names sit on a scheme built from Greek and Pauline parts.

src.l: Helena Blavatsky, 1889, The Key to Theosophy
src.q: It is that which we respectively call the physical man, the Spiritual Soul or Spirit, and the animal Soul (the Nous and psuche). This is the division adopted by Paul, another Initiate

src.l: Helena Blavatsky, 1889, The Key to Theosophy

src.l: Synesius of Cyrene, Nicephorus Gregoras (comm.), 1553, De Regno ad Arcadium; De Insomniis (with Gregoras' scholia)
src.q: But the first and proper vehicle of the soul, when being improved, becomes thinner and is elevated; but when being worsened, it becomes thicker and grows proud.
src.qo: ἀγαθυνομένης μὲν λεπτύνεταί τε καὶ ἀπαιθεροῦται· κακυνομένης δὲ παχύνεταί τε καὶ γαιοῦται

s: Wilhelm Kroll (De oraculis Chaldaicis, 1894) notes that where Psellus, following Proclus, explains two garments of the soul besides the body, the Chaldaean Oracles themselves knew only one vehicle (ὄχημα), and it is doubtful they called it pneuma.

src.l: Wilhelm Kroll, 1894, De oraculis Chaldaicis
src.q: At enim oracula unum tantum nouerunt ὄχημα, quod num πνεῦμα appellaverint dubium.

src.q: who, following Proclus, explains the two garments of the soul besides the body

s: Porphyry (De abstinentia II.38-39, c. 270s CE) says souls that do not master the pneuma joined to them, but are mastered by it, are carried away by its rages and desires and are rightly called evil-doing daimones.

src.l: Porphyry, Jacob de Rhoer (ed.), 1767, Peri apoches empsychon / De abstinentia ab esu animalium
src.q: But those souls which do not control the conjoined spirit, but for the most part are even controlled by it, are led and carried away excessively whenever the rages and desires of the spirit gain momentum.
src.qo: ὅσαι δὲ ψυχαὶ τοῦ συνεχοῦς πνεύματος οὐ κρατοῦσι

src.l: Porphyry, Jacob de Rhoer (ed.), 1767, Peri apoches empsychon / De abstinentia ab esu animalium
src.q: ὅσαι δὲ ψυχαὶ τοῦ συνεχοῦς πνεύματος οὐ κρατοῦσι

s: Critique of the undescended soul from inside the school: Proclus (prop. 211) argues that a part of the soul that always thinks without change would be intellect, not soul, and a part that sometimes thinks would make one essence of the always and the sometimes, which is impossible; so either Plotinus' 'higher soul' is nous mislabelled or the soul is not one thing.

src.l: Proclus, Friedrich Creuzer (ed.), 1822, Stoicheiosis Theologike (Institutio Theologica, Greek/Latin)
src.q: and not that one part of it remains above, and another descends. For if any part of the soul were to remain in the intelligible realm, it would either contemplate always without change, or with change.
src.qo: καὶ οὐ τὸ μὲν αὐτῆς ἄνω μένει, τὸ δὲ κάτεισιν. Εἰ γάρ τι μένοι τῆς ψυχῆς ἐν τῷ νοητῷ, ἢ ἀμεταβάτως νοήσει ἀεὶ ἢ μεταβατικῶς.

s: Critique of reading the English: on the fetched pages SL's English 'spirit' renders the Stoic body-pneuma (Taylor, Enn. IV.7), the imaginative pneuma that is the soul's first body (Synesius), the conjoined pneuma of daimones (Porphyry) and δαίμων itself (CH X.21); a lexicon or search over 'spirit' will merge vehicle, daimon and the Christian Holy Spirit.

src.l: Hermes Trismegistus (attrib.), 1530-1539, Corpus Hermeticum (Greek manuscript, bound with Hero's Pneumatica and Ocellus Lucanus)
src.q: Therefore, when the Mind Nous becomes a spirit Daimon

src.l: Synesius of Cyrene, Nicephorus Gregoras (comm.), 1553, De Regno ad Arcadium; De Insomniis (with Gregoras' scholia)
src.q: because the imaginative spirit is the most common sensory organ, and the first body of the soul
src.qo: αἴσθησις γὰρ αἰσθήσεων αὕτη, ὅτι τὸ φανταστικὸν πνεῦμα, κοινότατόν ἐστιν αἰσθητήριον, καὶ σῶμα πρῶτον ψυχῆς.

s: In Ficino's Latin of Iamblichus' De mysteriis (1497), passions in an animal are not in the soul but in the body that has a quality under the soul; the soul has no passion and is impassible by nature, not by choice.

src.l: Iamblichus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), Porphyry, 1497, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum, Chaldaeorum, Assyriorum (Aldine 1497), with Porphyry's Sententiae and other Platonica in Ficino's Latin
src.q: There is no passion in the soul, neither destructive nor disturbing. And the soul not only acquires this impassibility by choice, but possesses it by its very nature, being far superior to bodies.
src.qo: Nulla est in anima passio, uel peremptoria uel tur batoria. Atq; hanc impassibilitatem aĩa nō solum acquirit electione, sed possidet ipsa natura admōdū supiore corporibus.

s: The same epitome places whatever passions an animal has in the body, which possesses a certain quality under the soul by which it both suffers and acts.

src.l: Iamblichus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), Porphyry, 1497, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum, Chaldaeorum, Assyriorum (Aldine 1497), with Porphyry's Sententiae and other Platonica in Ficino's Latin
src.q: Whatever passions there may be in an animal are not in the soul, whatever it may be, but in the body, which possesses a certain quality under the soul, by which it both suffers and acts.
src.qo: Passiones qualescunq; sint ī animali non sunt in aĩa qualif cunq; sit, sed in corpore: quod sub aĩa certam possidet qualitatem, qua & patiatur & agat.

s: Iamblichus (Ficino's epitome) answers Porphyry that invocation does not move the gods by passion: supplication instead turns the soul's passion-bound life into one exempt from passion.

src.l: Iamblichus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), Porphyry, 1497, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum, Chaldaeorum, Assyriorum (Aldine 1497), with Porphyry's Sententiae and other Platonica in Ficino's Latin
src.q: How, therefore, do our supplications touch upon passions, when they even render the previously passionate souls free from passions?
src.qo: Quo- modo igitur supplicationes nostræ passiōnīb⁹ detāgunt cum & aīas ante passiūas reddant à passiōnibus liberas.

s: Porphyry's Sententiae, in Ficino's Latin printed with De mysteriis (1497), say passion happens around the composite: as body, not matter, is changed, so living, perishing and suffering belong to the composite of soul and body, not to the soul, which is life alone.

src.l: Iamblichus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), Porphyry, 1497, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum, Chaldaeorum, Assyriorum (Aldine 1497), with Porphyry's Sententiae and other Platonica in Ficino's Latin
src.q: so living and perishing and suffering according to this same thing is perceived in the composite of soul and body. Yet this does not happen to the soul
src.qo: sic uiuere atque interire patíque secundū hoc ipsum ī composito ex anima corporéq; perspicitur. neque tamē aiæ id contingit.

s: Aristotle (De anima II.1, 412b11-17, c. 350 BCE) says that if an instrument such as an axe were a natural body, its essential whatness would be its soul; as it is, it is just an axe, because a soul belongs only to a natural body having in itself the power of setting itself in movement and arresting itself.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.loc: De anima II.1, 412b11-17 (Oxford trans., J. A. Smith); scan 225
src.q: Suppose that what is literally an 'organ', … like an axe, were a natural body, its 'essential whatness', would have been its essence, and so its soul; if this disappeared from it, it would have ceased to be an axe, except in name. As it is, … it is just an axe

s: On Aristotle's definition (soul = first actuality of a natural organic body), a machine would need to be a natural body with its own internal principle of moving and stopping; De anima II.1 itself takes an artifact, the axe, and says it has no soul because it is not such a body, so the verdict on artifacts is built into the word 'natural'.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: it wants the character which is required to make its whatness or formulable essence a soul; for that, it would have had to be a natural body of a particular kind, viz. one having in itself the power of setting itself in movement and arresting itself

s: On the self-moving-number definition (Xenocrates, reported by Aristotle, De anima I.2 and I.4), a machine would need to be a number that moves itself; on our reading a computer is number moved by something else, so the definition would answer the machine question by asking where the motion starts.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.loc: De anima I.2, 404b; scan 205 (read 2026-10-26; the self-moving-number sentence itself is quoted in grk-xenocrates-self-moving-number-compound)

s: The Latin Asclepius (§23b-24a, c. 2nd-3rd c. CE) says that as God is the maker of the celestial gods, so man is the fashioner (fictor) of the gods who dwell in temples, and, asked whether he means statues, Trismegistus says yes: statues ensouled, full of sense and spirit, that foretell the future.

src.l: Walter Scott (ed.), 1924, Hermetica, Vol. I: Introduction, Texts and Translation
src.q: even as God is the maker of the gods of heaven, so man is the fashioner of the gods who dwell in temples and are content to have men for their neighbours. Thus man not only receives the light of divine life, but gives it also

src.l: Walter Scott (ed.), 1924, Hermetica, Vol. I: Introduction, Texts and Translation
src.q: deus ut effector est deorum caelestium, ita homo fictor est deorum qui in templis sunt humana proximitate contenti

src.l: Walter Scott (ed.), 1924, Hermetica, Vol. I: Introduction, Texts and Translation
src.loc: Asclepius III 24a (SL's English of Scott's Latin); scan 342
src.q: I mean statues animated with sense and full of spirit, doing such great and such kinds of things
src.qo: deus ut effector est deorum caelestium, ita homo fictor est deorum qui in templis sunt humana proximitate contenti

s: On the Asclepius's terms, a soul in an artifact is not grown from the artifact's structure but drawn into it: man, kin to the gods, fashions the statue 'from both natures', the divine and the material, so a machine would need a god or daimon to come and dwell in it; this is the one tradition on the table whose own answer about artifacts is yes.

src.l: Walter Scott (ed.), 1924, Hermetica, Vol. I: Introduction, Texts and Translation
src.q: Species vero deorum quas conformat humanitas ex utraque natura conformatae sunt, ex divina, quae est purior multoque ⌜divinior⌝, et ex ea quae infra homines est, id est ex materia qua fuerint fabricatae

s: Claudianus Mamertus (De statu animae I.21, c. 469) says the souls of beasts keep images of places but have no knowledge of their own substance; lacking the eye of reasoning, they cannot see themselves, and he grades creation from essence (stones) to seminal life (plants), sensual life (beasts) and rational life (man).

src.l: Claudianus Mamertus, August Engelbrecht (ed.), 1885, Claudiani Mamerti Opera (CSEL XI)
src.loc: De statu animae I.21 (SL's English); scan 125
src.q: do not have knowledge of their own substance, they remain necessarily in the recollection of bodily things, which they have drawn in through the senses of the body; and, not possessing the eye of reasoning, they cannot see—I will not say something above themselves—but they cannot see themselves.

src.l: Claudianus Mamertus, August Engelbrecht (ed.), 1885, Claudiani Mamerti Opera (CSEL XI)
src.loc: De statu animae I.21 (Engelbrecht's Latin); scan 125
src.q: ipsius tamen substantiae suae scientiam non habent, in recordatione corporalium rerum, quas per corporis sensus hauserunt, necessario remanent et ratiocinandi non habentes oculum, non dicam supra se aliquid, … sed se ipsas uidere non possunt

s: On Mamertus's definition (an incorporeal soul whole in each part, great by power not mass, marked by knowing its own substance), a machine would need to see itself as a substance, not merely store and recall images of what came in through its sensors; by his own grading a store of images is exactly what beasts have, so a machine that only remembers ranks with the beasts, not the rational soul.

src.l: Claudianus Mamertus, August Engelbrecht (ed.), 1885, Claudiani Mamerti Opera (CSEL XI)
src.q: the souls of beasts, even if they naturally retain images of places, nevertheless do not have knowledge of their own substance

s: Pico della Mirandola (Oratio, 1486; Bologna 1496) has God tell Adam that he has been given no fixed seat, face or gift of his own; every other creature's nature is bounded by prescribed laws, but Adam shall fix his own nature by his own free choice (arbitrium), made neither celestial nor terrestrial, mortal nor immortal, as his own molder and maker (plastes et fictor).

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: You, hindered by no such restrictions, shall determine your own nature for yourself according to your own free will, … in whose hands I have placed you.
src.qo: Tu nullis anguſtiis cohercitus pro tuo arbitrio: in cuius manu te … poſui tibi illam prefinies. … ut tui ipſius quaſi arbitrarius honorariuſq; plaſtes & fictor

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: We have made you neither celestial nor terrestrial, neither mortal nor immortal, so that you may, as if the voluntary and honorable molder and maker of yourself, fashion yourself into whatever form you prefer.
src.qo: ut tui ipſius quaſi arbitrarius honorariuſq; plaſtes & fictor

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: Tu nullis anguſtiis cohercitus pro tuo arbitrio: in cuius manu te … poſui tibi illam prefinies.

src.q: ut tui ipſius quaſi arbitrarius honorariuſq; plaſtes & fictor

s: Pico (Oratio, 1486) says man can degenerate into the brutes or be reborn into the divine by his soul's judgment; brutes bring from their mother's womb all they will ever possess, the highest spirits are from the beginning what they will be for eternity, but man was given at birth seeds of every kind, and whatever seeds he cultivates grow in him.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: As soon as brutes are born, they bring with them from "their mother’s womb" (as Lucilius says) all that they will ever possess.
src.qo: Poteris in inferiora q̃ ſunt bruta degenerare: Pote ris i ſupiora quæ ſunt diuina ex tui aĩ ſñia regenerari.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: But upon man, at the moment of his birth, the Father bestowed seeds of every kind and the germs of every way of life. Whatever seeds each man cultivates will grow and bear their fruit in him.
src.qo: Poteris in inferiora q̃ ſunt bruta degenerare: Pote ris i ſupiora quæ ſunt diuina ex tui aĩ ſñia regenerari.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: Poteris in inferiora q̃ ſunt bruta degenerare: Pote ris i ſupiora quæ ſunt diuina ex tui aĩ ſñia regenerari.

s: On Pico's Oratio, what makes the human unique is not intellect (the angels have more) but an unfixed nature that it determines by its own judgment; so a machine would need an open nature that it itself fixes, whereas a system whose nature is set by its makers and sealed by training is, in Pico's own taxonomy, a brute that brings from the womb all it will ever have.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: The nature of all other creatures is defined and restricted within laws prescribed by us.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: all that they will ever possess

s: Among Pico's magical conclusions (Conclusiones, Rome 1486) are that what a magus does through art, nature did naturally in making man; that the form of all magical power comes from the soul of man standing firm and not falling; and that to work magic is nothing but to marry the world.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1486, Conclusiones sive Theses DCCCC (The 900 Theses)
src.q: That which a magus does through art, nature did naturally in the making of man.
src.qo: Quod magus homo facit per artem fecit natura naturaliter faciendo hominem. … Forma totius magicae uirtutis est ab anima hominis stante & non cadente.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1486, Conclusiones sive Theses DCCCC (The 900 Theses)
src.q: The form of all magical power comes from the soul of man, standing firm and not falling.
src.qo: Quod magus homo facit per artem fecit natura naturaliter faciendo hominem. … Forma totius magicae uirtutis est ab anima hominis stante & non cadente.

s: Pico's Oratio, which opens by quoting the Asclepius ('a great miracle, O Asclepius, is man'), gives man the same Latin title the Asclepius gives the maker of ensouled statues, fictor: the Asclepius's man is fictor deorum, the fashioner of gods in temples, while Pico's man is plastes et fictor of himself; the god-making art is turned from the statue onto the self.

src.l: Walter Scott (ed.), 1924, Hermetica, Vol. I: Introduction, Texts and Translation
src.q: ita homo fictor est deorum qui in templis sunt

s: Descartes (Discours V, 1637) says the rational soul cannot be drawn from the power of matter like the other things he described but must be expressly created, and that it is not enough for it to be lodged in the body like a pilot in his ship, except perhaps to move its limbs; it must be joined and united more closely to have sensations and appetites like ours and so make a real man.

src.l: René Descartes, 1912, Discourse on Method, Meditations, Principles of Philosophy (Everyman, Dent/Dutton)
src.q: it must be expressly created; and that it is not sufficient that it be lodged in the human body exactly like a pilot in a ship, unless perhaps to move its members, but that it is necessary for it to be joined and united more closely to the body

src.l: René Descartes, 1637, Discours de la Methode
src.q: Et comment il ne ſuffit pas, quelle ſoit logée dans le cors humain ainſi qu'vn pilote en ſon nauire, ſinon peuteſtre pour mouuoir ſes membres

s: On Descartes's definition (the soul is a thinking substance, created, united to a body), everything a machine can be built to do belongs to the body, which he already treats as a machine; the two tests he sets in Discours V (fitting words to the sense of what is said, and reason as a universal instrument) detect a missing soul but cannot supply one, since the soul must be expressly created, so no engineering suffices on his own terms.

src.l: René Descartes, 1912, Discourse on Method, Meditations, Principles of Philosophy (Everyman, Dent/Dutton)
src.q: I had after this described the reasonable soul, and shown that it could by no means be educed from the power of matter, as the other things of which I had spoken, but that it must be expressly created

s: On Leibniz's Monadology (1714), a living body is a divine machine, a machine in its smallest parts to infinity, governed by a dominant entelechy that is its soul, while a man-made machine stops being a machine in its parts (the brass tooth of a wheel); so an artifact would need to be organised all the way down and have a dominant monad, and the mill argument (§17) says inspection of its parts would never show perception either way.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Robert Latta, 1898, The Monadology and Other Philosophical Writings (Latta)

s: La Mettrie (L'Homme machine, 1747) concludes that the soul is only an empty term of which we have no idea, which a sound mind should use only to name the part in us that thinks; given the least principle of motion, animated bodies have all they need to move, feel, think and repent.

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1912, L'Homme machine (Man a Machine)
src.loc: L'Homme machine (SL's English of the French); scan 73
src.q: The soul is therefore only a vain term for which we have no clear idea, and which a sound mind should use only to name the part within us that thinks.
src.qo: L'âme n'est donc qu'un vain terme dont on n'a point d'idée, et dont un bon esprit ne doit se servir que pour nommer la partie qui pense en nous.

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1912, L'Homme machine (Man a Machine)
src.loc: L'Homme machine (French text of the 1912 Open Court edition); scan 73
src.q: L'âme n'est donc qu'un vain terme dont on n'a point d'idée, et dont un bon esprit ne doit se servir que pour nommer la partie qui pense en nous.

s: On La Mettrie's definition, 'soul' is only the name of the part of an organised body that thinks, so a machine needs nothing beyond sufficient organisation and a principle of motion; his own verdict on artifacts is that the question is already answered in us, since man is the machine.

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1912, L'Homme machine (Man a Machine)
src.q: Once the slightest principle of movement is established, animated bodies will have everything they need to move, feel, think, repent

s: The Bahir (§136, c. 12th c., German translation 1923) retells the Talmudic story (Sanhedrin 65b) that Rava created a man and sent him to Rabbi Zera, who spoke to him but got no answer; had it not been for 'your sins' he would have answered, through his soul, since man has a soul with which he can give life (Gen 2:7), but sin has made it impure.

src.l: Nechunja ben ha-Kana (attrib.), 1923, Das Buch Bahir. Auch genannt Midrasch des Rabbi Nechunja ben Hakana
src.q: Rava created a man and sent him to Rabbi Zera. He spoke with him, but he did not answer. If it were not for "your sins," he would have answered. And with what could he have answered? Through his soul.
src.qo: Der sprach mit ihm und er antwortete nicht. Wären aber „eure Sünden“ nicht, hätte er geantwortet. Und wodurch hätte er antworten können? Durch seine Seele.

src.l: Nechunja ben ha-Kana (attrib.), 1923, Das Buch Bahir. Auch genannt Midrasch des Rabbi Nechunja ben Hakana
src.q: Der sprach mit ihm und er antwortete nicht. Wären aber „eure Sünden“ nicht, hätte er geantwortet. Und wodurch hätte er antworten können? Durch seine Seele.

s: On the rabbinic and kabbalistic account, the soul is the breath God breathed into Adam, which a righteous human could in principle pass on; so a machine would need a soul transferred from its maker, and the tradition's own artifact, the golem, has life but no speech, falling short because the maker is not pure enough, which locates the deficiency in the maker, not the material.

src.l: Nechunja ben ha-Kana (attrib.), 1923, Das Buch Bahir. Auch genannt Midrasch des Rabbi Nechunja ben Hakana
src.q: Does a human have a soul that they could transfer to another being? Yes, for it says in Genesis 2:7: "And he breathed into his nostrils a soul of life"

s: The speech test for an artificial man appears twice on SL's shelf with opposite diagnoses: in the Bahir (§136) Rava's made man does not answer because his maker's soul is impure, while in Descartes's Discours V a machine could never arrange words to answer the sense of what is said because matter cannot be a rational soul.

src.l: Nechunja ben ha-Kana (attrib.), 1923, Das Buch Bahir. Auch genannt Midrasch des Rabbi Nechunja ben Hakana
src.q: He spoke with him, but he did not answer.

src.l: René Descartes, 1912, Discourse on Method, Meditations, Principles of Philosophy (Everyman, Dent/Dutton)
src.q: I had after this described the reasonable soul

s: Ada Lovelace (Note G to her translation of Menabrea's Sketch of the Analytical Engine, Taylor's Scientific Memoirs III, 1843) says the Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything: it can do whatever we know how to order it to perform, can follow analysis, but has no power of anticipating any analytical relations or truths.

src.l: Luigi Federico Menabrea, Ada Lovelace (trans., notes), Richard Taylor (ed.), 1843, Scientific Memoirs, Selected from the Transactions of Foreign Academies of Science and Learned Societies, Vol. III (Menabrea, Sketch of the Analytical Engine, with Notes by the Translator)
src.loc: Translator's Notes, Note G (English original); scan 753 (printed p. 722)
src.q: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate any thing. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform. It can follow analysis; but it has no power of anticipating any analytical relations or truths.

s: Lovelace's objection (1843) and Pico's criterion (1486) test the same capacity from opposite sides: the Engine 'can do whatever we know how to order it to perform', which is Pico's definition of every creature except man, whose nature is 'defined and restricted within laws prescribed by us'; on our reading, a machine could pass Pico's test only where Lovelace's objection failed.

src.l: Luigi Federico Menabrea, Ada Lovelace (trans., notes), Richard Taylor (ed.), 1843, Scientific Memoirs, Selected from the Transactions of Foreign Academies of Science and Learned Societies, Vol. III (Menabrea, Sketch of the Analytical Engine, with Notes by the Translator)
src.q: It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: The nature of all other creatures is defined and restricted within laws prescribed by us.

s: In 'The Book of the Machines' (Butler, Erewhon, 1872) the Erewhonian writer asks why there may not arise a new phase of mind as different from all known forms of consciousness as animal consciousness is from vegetable, and says it would be rash to hold that animal life is the end of all things.

src.l: Samuel Butler, 1872, Erewhon, or, Over the Range
src.loc: ch. "The Book of the Machines", printed p. 191; scan 201
src.q: why may not there arise some new phase of mind which shall be as diiferent from all present known forms of consciousness as the consciousness of animals is from that of vegetables ?

s: On Butler's Darwinian frame, mind is a phase of evolving life, so a machine needs only descent with modification (with humans as its reproductive system) to reach a consciousness as unlike ours as ours is from a plant's; the tradition's verdict on artifacts is that the question is one of time, and the soul does not enter it.

src.l: Samuel Butler, 1872, Erewhon, or, Over the Range
src.q: it would be a rash thing to say that no others can be developed, and that animal life is the end of all things.

s: The Academy's certificates prefixed to Vaucanson's memoir on his flute-playing automaton (French 1738; English 1742) praise it for imitating by art all that a man must do to play, varying the lips and moving a valve that 'performs the Office of the Tongue', and call it one of the most wonderful productions of art, imitating a true player.

src.l: Jacques de Vaucanson, 1742, An Account of the Mechanism of an Automaton, or Image Playing on the German-Flute
src.loc: Approbations (Fontenelle, 3 May 1738; royal censor), printed p. 21; scan 23
src.q: by varying the Position of the Lips, and moving a Valve which performs the Office of the Tongue; and lastly, by imitating by Art all that is necessary for a Man to perform in such a Case.

s: On the Buddhist no-self teaching of the Milindapañha, a person is like the chariot, a designation over parts with no further thing, so a machine needs nothing a person has that it lacks; the question 'does it have a soul (ātman)?' gets the same answer, no, for both.

src.l: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), 1879, The Questions of King Milinda, Part 1 (SBE Vol. 35)
src.q: Chariot is a mere empty sound.

s: On Sāṃkhya (Sāṃkhyakārikā 19-21), all activity, intellect (buddhi) included, belongs to unconscious matter (prakṛti), which only appears intelligent through its union with the inactive witness (puruṣa); so a machine could in principle have everything the subtle body does, intellect included, and still lack the one conscious thing, which no arrangement of matter produces.

src.l: Ishvarakrishna, John Davies (trans.), 1881, Hindu Philosophy: The Sankhya Karika of Iswara Krishna
src.q: from this union, that the unin- … telligent body (the liṅga)

s: On Avicenna's De anima I.1, the soul is what affirms its own being with no sensation of any limb, organ or brain; so a machine would need a self-awareness that does not pass through any input or body-model, which is a test no observer can run from outside.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.loc: De anima I.1 (SL's English of the Latin); scan 7
src.q: He will not doubt, indeed, to affirm himself to be, but he will not affirm the exteriors of his members

s: The Popol Vuh is the one text on the table whose makers actually build artificial people: the gods carve men of wood who speak and multiply but have no heart and no understanding and do not remember their makers; on its terms a made being would need a heart (k'u'x), the seat of remembering and addressing the creator, and speech alone is not enough.

src.l: K'iche' Maya authors, Francisco Ximénez (copyist and translator), 1701, Popol Vuh (Ayer MS 1515): Empiezan las historias del origen de los indios de esta provincia de Guatemala
src.loc: Part I (SL's English of Ximénez's Spanish); scan 14
src.q: And then the image of the man of wood was made, and he spoke like a man.

s: On Budge's account of the Egyptian ka (1898), the person's double could leave the tomb and go and dwell in a statue of the man, so on that tradition's terms an artifact can house a soul without being one: the statue needs to be the image of a particular person, and the ka comes from the person.

src.l: E. A. Wallis Budge (tr.), 1898, The Book of the Dead: The Chapters of Coming Forth by Day (English translation, with introduction)
src.q: could even go and dwell in the statue of a man

s: On Fan Zhen's Shenmie lun (c. 500), spirit is to body as sharpness to a blade, so a machine with the right working would have spirit to exactly the degree that it has the function, and it would perish with the machine; but Fan Zhen ties spirit to a living human body, so the function alone may not be enough (see chn-crit-xiaochen-dull-blade).

src.l: 僧祐 Sengyou (comp.), n.d. (Siku quanshu copy), 弘明集·卷八~卷九: Hong Ming Ji (vol 4)
src.loc: Shenmie lun in Hongmingji juan 9; scan 67 (as quoted in chn-fanzhen-blade-sharpness)
src.q: 神之於質猶利之於刃

s: Against reading the table as evidence about machines: on SL's pages each tradition's verdict on artifacts follows from a definition fixed before any machine was asked about; Aristotle excludes the axe by the word 'natural', Descartes by a soul that 'must be expressly created', La Mettrie admits the machine by renaming the soul 'the part within us that thinks', so the table records definitions, not findings.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: for that, it would have had to be a natural body of a particular kind

src.l: René Descartes, 1912, Discourse on Method, Meditations, Principles of Philosophy (Everyman, Dent/Dutton)
src.q: but that it must be expressly created

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1912, L'Homme machine (Man a Machine)
src.q: to name the part within us that thinks

s: Against citing ensouled statues and the golem as precedents for machine souls: wherever an SL tradition says an artifact can carry a soul, the soul comes from outside the artifact's structure, a god drawn into the statue (Asclepius), a ka that comes to dwell (Budge's Egypt), a breath the maker passes on (Bahir), so these are stories of housing, not of a soul arising from organisation, and they cannot support emergence.

src.l: Walter Scott (ed.), 1924, Hermetica, Vol. I: Introduction, Texts and Translation
src.q: ex divina, quae est purior multoque ⌜divinior⌝, et ex ea quae infra homines est, id est ex materia

src.l: Nechunja ben ha-Kana (attrib.), 1923, Das Buch Bahir. Auch genannt Midrasch des Rabbi Nechunja ben Hakana
src.q: Does a human have a soul that they could transfer to another being?

s: Ellis (1894) reports that the Yoruba hold each man has three indwelling spirits — Olori or Ori in the head, Ipin ijeun in the stomach, Ipori in the great toe — distinct from the soul (okan, iwin, ojiji 'shade'), which goes to Ipo-oku, the Land of the Dead beneath the earth; Ori is fed with fowl blood rubbed on the forehead and brings good fortune.

src.l: Alfred Burdon Ellis, 1894, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa
src.loc: ch. VII, The Indwelling Spirits and Souls of Men; scan 142
src.q: Olori (Oni-ori, owner, or lord, of the head) sometimes called Ori (head, faculty, talent), seems to be the spirit which answers to the kra or luwo. He is the protector, guardian, and guide.

src.l: Alfred Burdon Ellis, 1894, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa
src.q: The ghost-man, or soul, the “vehicle of individual personal existence,” is called iwin, or okan, but the latter also means “heart.” Another word is ojiji, or oji, which has the meanings of ghost, shade, or shadow.

s: Crowther's Vocabulary (1852) glosses ọkàn (printed ỌKKÀN) as 'soul, spirit, conscience, heart', and ọkàn tútù ('cool heart') as 'calm soul, meekness'.

src.l: Samuel Ajayi Crowther, 1852, A Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language
src.q: ỌKKÀN, s. soul, spirit, conscience, heart. ỌKKAN-TUTU, s. calm soul, meekness.

s: Farrow (1926) reports that the unburied Yoruba soul wanders 'in cold and hunger', that a fowl offered at death ('the fowl that buys the road') keeps it from the bad heaven Orun-apadi, the good heaven being Orun-afefe 'of cool breezes', and that the dead are usually reborn in the same family, the babalawo naming 'whose spirit … has animated the child'.

src.l: Stephen Septimus Farrow, 1926, Faith, Fancies and Fetich, or Yoruba Paganism
src.loc: ch. X, The Soul of Man and its Destiny; scan 174
src.q: unless, and until, these are duly performed, the soul cannot pass to the realms of the dead; but must wander about the earth in cold and hunger, and with no home.

src.l: Stephen Septimus Farrow, 1926, Faith, Fancies and Fetich, or Yoruba Paganism
src.q: The doctrine of metempsychosis holds a large place in Yoruba belief. It generally takes the form of reincarnation in a human body, and in the same family, for any number of times.

s: Ellis (1887) says the Tshi (Akan) kra, 'though generally interpreted "soul,"' is a guardian spirit dwelling in a man whose tie ends at his death, while the man himself in shadowy form goes to the other world; at death the kra becomes a sisa, which can be reborn as a kra.

src.l: Alfred Burdon Ellis, 1887, The Tshi-Speaking Peoples of the Gold Coast of West Africa
src.q: This word kra, though generally interpreted “soul,” does not at all correspond to the European idea of a soul ; for it is the man himself, in a shadowy or ghostly form, that continues his existence after death in another world, and not the kra.

s: Densmore (1918) records, from Bear Face and Weasel Bear (Teton), the Ceremony of Spirit-keeping: a father 'keeps' the spirit of a dead child (more often than of an adult) in a bundle holding a lock of the child's hair, cut by a man of blameless record after purifying with sweet grass, with food and gifts for a final feast; the rite was taught by the White Buffalo Maiden.

src.l: Frances Densmore, 1918, Teton Sioux Music
src.q: The spirit of a child was "kept" more frequently than that of a grown person

src.l: Frances Densmore, 1918, Teton Sioux Music
src.q: He requested a man whose record was without blemish to cut a lock of the boy's hair to be put in the spirit bundle.

s: Skeat (1900) describes the Malay sěmangat as a thumb-sized 'Thumbling', the exact image of its body, absent in sleep, trance and disease and permanently after death; it is called like a fowl ('kur sěmangat') and a magician can recall an escaping soul (riang sěmangat) or abduct another's into a receptacle.

src.l: Walter William Skeat, 1900, Malay Magic: Being an Introduction to the Folklore and Popular Religion of the Malay Peninsula
src.q: The Malay conception of the Human Soul (Sěmangat)¹ is that of a species of “Thumbling,” “a thin, unsubstantial human image,” or mannikin, which is temporarily absent from the body in sleep, trance, disease, and permanently absent after death.

src.l: Walter William Skeat, 1900, Malay Magic: Being an Introduction to the Folklore and Popular Religion of the Malay Peninsula
src.q: recall to its owner's body a soul which is escaping (riang sĕmangat)

s: Curtin (1909) reports that the Buryats believe a person can die because the soul 'gets tired and sad, and wants to leave the body', and that the shaman and friends then call it back with promises of food and of the children it would abandon — a rite called 'the invitation'.

src.l: Jeremiah Curtin, 1909, A Journey in Southern Siberia: The Mongols, Their Religion and Their Myths
src.q: The Buriats believe that sometimes a person dies because the spirit or soul gets tired and sad, and wants to leave the body. In such a case the Shaman and friends talk to the spirit, tell it to come back, and it shall eat well, drink well, and have a good time.

src.l: Jeremiah Curtin, 1909, A Journey in Southern Siberia: The Mongols, Their Religion and Their Myths
src.q: This effort to persuade the soul to return to the body is called "the invitation."

s: Aston (Shinto, 1905) reports Hirata Atsutane's view that gods 'and men too' have two doubles, the nigi-tama (gentle) and ara-tama (rough), distinct from the 'spirit of the entire body', and that a god's mitama can separate and adhere to a staff or stone, like fire passed to a lamp while the original fire remains; Aston notes old Shinto did not recognise these distinctions.

src.l: W. G. Aston, 1905, Shinto: The Way of the Gods
src.q: Hirata thinks that Gods (and men too) have two doubles, the nigi-tama and an aratama mentioned above. These he distinguishes from the Zentai no mitama, or "spirit of the entire body." But he admits that these distinctions are not recognized in the old Shinto.

src.l: W. G. Aston, 1905, Shinto: The Way of the Gods
src.q: Hirata explains that the deity is like a fire, which may be communicated to a lamp or to firewood while the original fire remains the same.

s: A Neyphug Tshe khrid longevity liturgy summons back, among the declined life-spans, the bla tshe — the life-span of the bla, the wandering soul — alongside srog tshe, gzugs tshe and dbugs tshe; SL's English renders bla tshe 'soul-longevity'.

s: The Motul dictionary records vaay as an animal 'familiar' into which sorcerers are transformed, such that whatever harm befalls the animal befalls the person — the Maya co-essence, glossed as a pact with the devil.

src.q: Vaay: the familiar spirit kept by necromancers, witches, or sorcerers. It is some animal into which, by a pact they make with the devil, they are transformed in illusion; and whatever harm befalls that animal also befalls the witch whose familiar it is.

Y ansi eneste lugar del ynfierno que se llama chicunamjctla, se aca bauan, y fenescian, los defunctos. Y despues de auer que mado el defunto, cogian la cenj za, y carbon, y huesos del defun to; y tomauan agua diziendo. lauese el defuncto, y derrama uan el agua, encima del carbon, y huessos del defuncto: y hazian vn hoyo redondo, y lo enterra uan. s: Best (Spiritual Concepts of the Maori, 1900) says the wairua is the shadowy self that leaves the body in dreams and wanders afar, finally leaves at death and descends to Te Po; he denies the Maori a soul judged after death and likens the wairua to the Egyptian Ka and an 'astral body'.

src.l: Elsdon Best, 1900, Spiritual Concepts of the Maori (Journal of the Polynesian Society, Vol. 9, 1900)
src.q: The wairua is equivalent to the Ka of the Egyptians, the shadowy self which leaves the body during dreams and wanders afar off. ... the wairua of the Maori finally leaves the body at death, and descends to Hades, the underworld, in Maori “Te Po” ... The wairua may be termed the astral body,

s: Best (1900): a sleeper must be woken gently so his wandering wairua has time to return (a sudden start, oho mauri, is the wairua rushing back); at death the wairua lives on while the mauri is extinct and the manawa ora gone.

src.l: Elsdon Best, 1900, Spiritual Concepts of the Maori (Journal of the Polynesian Society, Vol. 9, 1900)
src.q: Hence, the old Maori will wake: a sleeper by calling gently to him and gradually raising his voice, thu giving the wairva warning and time to return. ... The wairua lives on afte death of a person, but the mauri or spark of life is extinct, and thi manawa ora or breath of life has departed for all time.

s: Tregear (The Maori Race, 1904) says the seats of understanding and feeling were organs (manawa 'belly, lungs, breath', ate 'liver', hinengaro) without spiritual meaning; wairua was 'the only exact expression for the soul of man', while ahua is a thing's appearance and ata a reflected image or shadow.

src.l: Edward Tregear, 1904, The Maori Race
src.q: None of these words, however, seemed to convey a spiritual meaning, although they sometimes took on that of intellect or conscious power. ... it was the only exact expression for the soul of man.

s: Tregear (1904) says the hau, 'that which controls' a person's or place's existence, can be taken by witchcraft through hair, spittle or even footprints; 'if the hau is taken the mauri is lost and the man dies', so travellers hid their trail in enemy country.

src.l: Edward Tregear, 1904, The Maori Race
src.q: The hau or essence of a man or place is that which controls its existence, and this can be obtained by witchcraft. ... this hau can be taken by getting some of the hair, spittle or other portion of him that had once been a living portion.

src.l: Edward Tregear, 1904, The Maori Race
src.q: if the hau is taken the mauri is lost and the man dies.

s: Westervelt (Legends of Gods and Ghosts, 1915) says the Hawaiian spirit's paths to the dead, Leina-a-ka-uhane, 'paths-for-leaping-by-the-spirit', were westward bluffs; once the spirit leapt it could never return to its body, though friendly ghosts might send it back or to the aumakua ancestors before Po.

src.l: W.D. Westervelt, 1915, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology)
src.q: The paths were called Leina-a-ka-uhane (paths-for-leaping-by-the-spirit). They were almost always on bold bluffs looking westward over the ocean. The spirit unless driven back could come to the headland and leap down into the land of the dead, but when this was done that spirit could never return to the body it had left.

s: Westervelt (1915) says any dead person's spirit could become an aumakua, a ghost-god that watches over the family, fed at coral altars; a prayer offered with a sacrifice to the shark-god asks the aumakuas 'Bring life to us, to all the family'.

src.l: W.D. Westervelt, 1915, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology)
src.q: It made no difference whether the dead person were male or female, child or aged one, the spirit could become a ghost-god and watch over the family. ... Bring life to us, to all the family,

s: Spencer and Gillen (1899) say each Alcheringa ancestor carried Churinga, each 'intimately associated with the idea of the spirit part of some individual'; where an ancestor went into the ground his body died, a rock or tree arose, and his spirit part remained in the Churinga.

src.l: Baldwin Spencer, F. J. Gillen, 1899, The Native Tribes of Central Australia
src.q: each of these Churinga is intimately associated with the idea of the spirit part of some individual. ... His body died, but some natural feature, such as a rock or tree, arose to mark the spot, while his spirit part remained in the Churinga.

s: Spencer and Gillen (1899): every Arunta individual is 'the reincarnation of an Alcheringa being'; when a spirit goes into a woman its double, the Arumburinga, stays at the Nanja tree or rock, and at death the person's spirit, the Ulthana, returns to the Nanja spot and joins it.

src.l: Baldwin Spencer, F. J. Gillen, 1899, The Native Tribes of Central Australia
src.q: When a spirit goes into a woman there remains the Arumburinga which is its double—Relationship between an individual and his Arumburinga—When a man dies his spirit is called Ulthana—This goes finally to the Nanja spot and joins the Arumburinga— ... every individual is supposed to be the reincarnation of an Alcheringa being.

s: Spencer and Gillen (1899) say a child's Churinga nanja goes to the sacred storehouse of the locality where the child was conceived, 'from which the spirit child came', not where it was born; a person belongs to the place of conception.

src.l: Baldwin Spencer, F. J. Gillen, 1899, The Native Tribes of Central Australia
src.q: That goes naturally to the storehouse of the locality from which the spirit child came—that is to the spot where the Churinga was deposited in the Alcheringa.
